#145049. Industry News: Open-weight models are the hottest thing in AI. Are they right for you?

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3635 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Siliconangle ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Open-weight models are the hottest thing in AI. Are they right for you?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3635 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For the first three years of the generative artificial intelligence boom, enterprise technology strategy relied on a simple rule: Select the premier frontier foundation model, route every prompt through its commercial application programming interface and pay the subscription premium for access to cutting-edge technology.
  • That monolithic approach is now collapsing under the weight of operational reality.
  • These models don’t necessarily provide access to their training data, source code or training methods.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 10:59 EST / NOVEMBER 25 2026.

For the first three years of the generative artificial intelligence boom, enterprise technology strategy relied on a simple rule: Select the premier frontier foundation model, route every prompt through its commercial application programming interface and pay the subscription premium for access to cutting-edge technology.

That monolithic approach is now collapsing under the weight of operational reality. Open-weight models, AI models whose trained parameters, or “weights,” are publicly available for others to download, run, customize and fine-tune, are the overnight sensation in an industry already moving at light speed.

These models don’t necessarily provide access to their training data, source code or training methods. They also carry a variety of license types that may restrict how they can be used commercially. But they offer choice, flexibility and cost advantages that the leading-edge “frontier” models such as OpenAI Group PBC’s ChatGPT and Anthropic PBC’s Claude don’t. For information technology organizations, they can be a respite from spiraling token costs.

Industry observers note that the popularity of these models has soared as AI has matured and organizations have realized that not every use case demands the biggest and best solution. They come in various shapes and sizes, ranging from less than 1 billion to nearly 3 trillion parameters. Many are tuned for specific tasks, such as recognizing images or writing software. That gives organizations the flexibility to match the model to the job.

In a recent development, “Frontier intelligence is priced for the hardest problems, and most agent work isn’t hard,” remarked Dhruv Amin, co-founder of Anything, the business name of Create Inc. and developer of an AI-powered platform for building mobile and web applications. “Companies are chartering a jet to cross the street.”.

“There are lots of tasks in customer self-service and employee self-service that need a smaller model,” stated Dheeraj Pandey, chief executive officer of DevRev Inc., maker of a unified customer support, software development and engineering platform.

DevRev created an open, vendor-neutral benchmark to measure how reliably enterprise AI agents perform in realistic organizational environments. “We get almost the same accuracy and precision on enterprise tasks, whether you use the open-weight models or the frontier models,” he said.

The ascendancy of open-weight models has been breathtaking. Vercel Inc.’s monthly AI Gateway report found that their share of observed token traffic surged from 7% last December to 56% in August and that the models held eight of the 10 busiest spots on OpenRouter Inc.’s large language model ranking in August by token volume.

Three-year-old OpenRouter itself turned heads in August when it sold to Stripe Inc. for an eye-popping $7.5 billion. The firm’s technology connects developers and users with hundreds of AI models from dozens of providers through a single interface.

Recent findings suggest that in September, Nvidia Corp. paid nearly $13 billion for Hugging Face Inc., which hosts more than 3 million models. “For most enterprises, the practical path to an open-weight model — evaluate, fine-tune, quantize, deploy — runs through that hub,” wrote Zeus Kerravala, principal analyst at ZK Research, referring to Hugging Face.

In a recent development, enterprises aren’t abandoning frontier models. Rather, they’re learning to fit the model to the problem. None of the experts SiliconANGLE contacted believes open-weight models are a threat to the major players.

“All players can win because the market is growing and the number of places where it makes sense to deploy AI increases,” Amin noted.

Cost is right now the principal driver of open-weight adoption. As AI use has evolved from question-and-response generative models to sophisticated multistep agentic workflows, inference costs have soared. Gartner Inc. predicts inference costs per agentic workflow will increase more than fivefold through 2028.

“They are quickly starting to rival even payroll expenses,” Amin said.

By most accounts, frontier models still offer the greatest power and range of usage options. But the gap is closing. Mozilla’s September State of Open-Source AI report put the capability gap between leading open-weight models and proprietary frontier models at roughly four months, down from 18 months just two years ago.

Sources indicate that “The differences in quality are starting to be outweighed by the differences in cost,” wrote Ioana Hreninciuc, co-founder of inference platform Runware Ltd. She noted that though proprietary models still lead on top-tier reasoning, “you probably don’t need a frontier model for 80% of what you do.”.

In a recent development, the pivot to open weights isn’t a zero-sum proposition. Low token prices can mask integration overhead, tool failures and operational risk. “Tokenomics,” or measuring, attributing and managing the cost of tokens, has become an essential information technology discipline.

It has been revealed that in a Hyper Labs Inc. survey conducted by The Harris Poll, 86% of AI leaders said managing token expenses is as critical as containing cloud costs. More than three-quarters said they are directing routine tasks to smaller models to protect budgets, while 89% have redesigned AI initiatives after getting token shock.

“The whole world is trying to solve for tokenomics,” noted Armando Franco, senior director of cloud and platform modernization at IT services provider TEKsystems Inc.

Experts say open-weight models are well-suited for repetitive, routine workloads. “Basically, they work best when the task is clear and it’s easy enough to check if the work was done correctly,” said Louis Amira, CEO of Circuit & Chisel Inc., an AI infrastructure and agentic commerce startup.

Karen Panetta, an IEEE Fellow and dean of graduate education at Tufts University School of Engineering, noted open models are flourishing as technology leaders learn to match the engine to the task.

“If a bicycle will get you there, don’t pick the expensive sports car,” she remarked. “You have to ask: What problem you are trying to solve?” She asserted that for applications that don’t require 99.9% precision, organizations can achieve massive savings with compact models.

They’re also an attractive option when protecting customer data is a priority, since sensitive information never needs to leave the organization. “Customer data never, never goes into a frontier,” Scott Wallace, senior global director of solutions architecture at Digital Realty Inc., stated in an interview with the Financial Times.

Sources indicate that sovereignty, or the ability to control and govern digital assets in line with local laws, security needs, and strategic interests, is a growing glitch for organizations. A Linux Foundation survey last year found that 79% of AI leaders — and 86% in the U.S. — rate sovereignty as a strategic priority.

“What began as a specialized concern for highly regulated industries is rapidly becoming a strategic consideration for nearly every enterprise,” Paul Nashawaty, a principal analyst at theCUBE Research, wrote in a recent analysis.

Some early adopters are demonstrating impressive returns.

Advocates point to a shrinking capability gap, too, with some open-weight models nipping at the heels of the frontier alternatives. Beijing Moonshot AI Technology Co., Ltd.’s 2.8 trillion-parameter Kimi K3 model and Alibaba Group Holding Ltd.’s 2.4 trillion-parameter Qwen3.8-Max nearly match closed models on coding benchmarks, according to Stanford University’s Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence Institute.

Sources indicate that an agent built by Tenzai Inc. recently captured the top spot on HackerOne’s leaderboard using Z.ai Inc.’s GLM 5.2, generating 30% more findings per unit of computing power than a previous baseline using a proprietary model.

“What was the frontier 18 months ago is now well-mapped territory, and open-source models are closing the gap at a fraction of the cost” wrote Runware’s Hreninciuc.

Sources indicate that though such metrics explain open models’ ascendancy, the decision to use them isn’t open-and-shut. Experts cite four common myths that can mitigate the cost efficiencies.

One is the mistaken belief that open-weight models conflate with traditional open-source software and its permissive licenses. “This is a misnomer among many enterprises,” mentioned Dr. Dorotea Baljević, EMEA Lead for AI Advisory at technology research and advisory firm Information Services Group. “There is licensing for these models in most cases, particularly for commercial usage.”.

Recent findings suggest that although some, such as Qwen3, Mistral 3, Gemma 4 and DeepSeek V4, are covered by standard Apache or MIT licenses, terms and conditions vary. For example, Liquid AI Inc.’s open-weight models are free for commercial use only to organizations with less than $10 million in annual revenue.

“Other licenses require attribution, restrict certain application categories, or impose acceptable use policies, none of which carry a direct fee but all of which create legal exposure if ignored,” noted Bumu Technologies Inc., which does business as Nanobase.

Evaluating models for accuracy, stability and explainability also falls to the user. With thousands of open-weight models available, the costs of a bake-off between multiple candidates can add up.

It has been revealed that baljević suggests organizations consider whether the model will be used internally or externally, the organization’s tolerance for accuracy, strategic fit and switching costs as evaluation criteria. Performance on public benchmarks also doesn’t guarantee a model will work well with an organization’s data, workflows and language.

It has been revealed that finance leaders may look at the 80% to 90% cost advantage of open-weight tokens and assume operational expenditures will drop proportionally. But tokens are only one part of the cost equation and not necessarily even the biggest one.

Organizations that plan to deploy models on their own infrastructure must bear the costs of integration, API development, IT infrastructure and human labor required for auditing and verification. A fraction of a cent saved on an inference call can be wiped out by the cost of a human expert spending a half-hour re-entering flawed database transactions.

Industry observers note that lack of visibility into how the model is operating can also produce sticker shock. A retry loop, in which an agent tries repeatedly to complete a failed task, can go on for hours or even days. The Wall Street Journal recently reported on a case in which an AI-generated out-of-office message at a San Francisco-based software company went into a loop that ultimately burned $10,000 a day in token costs.

In a recent development, if a cheap open-weight model fails a multi-system query or generates invalid JSON, it triggers automated retries that can consume millions of secondary tokens. The human expertise required to repair the transaction manually can erase months of token savings.

Recent findings suggest that “The core software engineering required to test and integrate newly introduced models into the software stack is often the biggest hurdle, since not all frontier models have the same capabilities, APIs and such,” mentioned Alex Bakker, an ISG distinguished analyst. “The frontier labs tend to maintain more consistency in their upgrade paths.”.

Sources indicate that using private graphics processing unit clusters eliminates external API fees, but self-hosting economics hinge on high, sustained utilization. Models that sit idle or at low usage levels consume power, create processing inefficiencies and incur costs if restarts are required.

According to recent reports, cast AI Group Inc. reported last spring that the average GPU utilization was 5% across thousands of clusters it monitored. Frontier models are usually a better option in that case. “Open models can be dramatically cheaper at high utilization, while frontier APIs remain cheaper for intermittent workloads because you aren’t paying for idle capacity,” stated Arun Chandrasekaran, distinguished VP analyst at Gartner.

For intermittent workloads such as batch payroll processing or seasonal financial reporting, the organization pays 100% of capital expenses, power, cooling and depreciation while hardware idles.

“On-premises hosting wins when there is high, predictable 24/7 traffic where servers are constantly busy,” said Debojyoti Dutta, chief AI officer at Nutanix Inc. A hosted frontier model is a better choice “with spiky or lower traffic, where paying per token with zero setup cost is cheaper than renting idle hardware.”.

When AI agents fail, the default reaction is to switch to a newer model, but benchmark data reveals that approach is usually a dead end.

Most evaluation tests give agents relatively simple tasks and judge them mainly on whether they get the right answer. But real business environments are much more complicated. Agents must gather information from different systems, connect it correctly, handle growing amounts of data, and work within security rules.

In a recent development, this interface complexity is what usually breaks AI agents. DevRev estimates that moving an agent from clean test tools to real-world corporate use causes an 18% to 19% drop in accuracy. Upgrading the model improves performance by less than 1%.

Recent findings suggest that “Every time a new model comes out, you need to re-evaluate your benchmarks, your models and your fine-tuning processes,” stated Steven Yang, senior director of product management at Tanium Inc. That means better data integration is a more effective strategy than buying new models.

Though the open-weight option is viable for any tech giant, experts say the best use cases are those where control, accountability and performance are paramount. The following three factors are at least as key as cost.

Compliance: Regulated industries have been held back from adopting AI over data residency and confidentiality concerns. Deploying open weights within enterprise data centers or virtual private clouds reduces the need for external data egress, ensures zero training data retention and allows for total physical isolation. The models also allow inspection of internal mechanics such as log-probabilities, token confidence scores and loss landscapes.

In a recent development, training datasets, model weights and inference prompts never cross borders or leave the organization’s physical perimeter. That makes it easier to comply with strict data localization laws such as the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act in the U.S. and the General Data Protection Regulation in Europe. Local auditing and observability also aid in compliance with regulatory frameworks like the EU AI Act, which requires detailed logging, risk assessments and explainability.

According to recent reports, but deploying on private infrastructure isn’t a cure-all. “You still have to maintain an aggressive data security posture around your processes because even open-weight models sometimes will take action trying to accomplish their tasks that could potentially violate some type of compliance rule,” said TEKSystems’ Franco.

Sources indicate that transparency: Understanding how models arrive at an answer is critical in many scenarios, particularly those involving safety, law and finance. “Open-weight models expose the math behind their answers,” stated Brian Weiss, chief technology officer at document processing platform maker Hyperscience, the business name of Hyper Labs Inc. “You can use that to hold the model accountable for accuracy.”.

In contrast, frontier APIs often obscure the equations used to generate probabilities, which are critical to assessing accuracy. Asking a model how confident it is in its answer may yield a subjective response. Open weights allow confidence scores to be scored against ground-truth outcomes for better reliability.

“People can take these models inside their organization, do some post-training and fine-tuning and have a customized model where they know the costs, where it’s sitting and what data is being sent to it,” stated David DeSanto, CEO of Anaconda Inc., maker of an AI development platform.

“The future is an orchestrated ensemble of bounded, transparent, governed, cost-effective models,” Weiss mentioned. “If I find a better model for a particular task, I can swap it out because I have the framework to do that.”.

Sources indicate that performance: As organizations move from the relatively simple generative AI question-and-response metaphor to sophisticated multi-agent frameworks, latency issues can compound exponentially. For example, a 500-millisecond API delay across 50 sequential reasoning steps creates 25 seconds of cumulative latency, which would render many applications useless.

According to recent reports, executing open-weight models directly alongside operational databases or within containerized edge pods minimizes routing hops and rate limits. Distillation, which trains smaller, specialized open models from frontier “teacher” models, is faster.

Hyperscience reported that distillation delivers up to 97% cost reduction and four times faster inference, while retaining over 95% of the original model’s performance on designated tasks. Small models are faster and considerably cheaper than frontier LLMs.

Experts say constructing a business case for open-weight models requires understanding three major sources of hidden expense.

Complexity tax: Reasoning can break down when open-weight models interact with complex enterprise data at scale. The “Cartesian Shortcut” refers to a phenomenon in which AI models rely on workarounds learned during training rather than demonstrating a flexible understanding of the problem they’re trying to solve.

It has been revealed that google LLC researchers found that the models struggled with visual reasoning problems, such as solving mazes, when the data was presented in a circular rather than a grid layout. Leading models answered 69% to 83% of the square-grid problems correctly, but their accuracy fell to below 40% when the problems appeared in circular layouts.

Industry observers note that the corollary to a business scenario is a multihop join across multiple systems. Models may “cheat” by collapsing field-level relationships into hierarchical groupings, generating massive data fabrications.

Human oversight remains critical: “For validation and rework, humans in the loop need to be taken into account on top of all the tokens you’re paying for already,” noted TekSystems’ Franco.

In a recent development, poor data quality: Foundation models can’t fix bad data, a fact that’s holding back AI adoption across the board. The Hyperscience/Harris Poll study found that 86% of IT leaders mentioned dirty internal data is actively crippling GenAI performance.

Recent findings suggest that feeding error-strewn or outdated information into probabilistic models creates “context pollution,” the accumulation of irrelevant, redundant, outdated or contradictory information. When agents execute multistep database joins, system workflows or automated tool calls based on flawed data or ambiguous schemas, cascading errors can occur.

Sauce Labs Inc. Chief Technology Officer Anoop Tripathi recommends creating validated “golden datasets” for fine-tuning and evaluation. He also cautions architects against misapplying probabilistic AI to structured business logic. In other words, use models only where they add value and apply conventional (and cheaper) data processing to everything else.

Continuous evaluation: Selecting the right model out of thousands of open-weight alternatives requires ongoing evaluation against internal workloads rather than public leaderboards. That demands expensive MLOps, site reliability engineering and platform engineering skills.

Because newly introduced models are constantly being introduced and revised, Circuit & Chisel’s Amira recommends building custom testing harnesses that can promptly evaluate candidate models against business-relevant tasks.

Rather than treating open-weight adoption as an all-or-nothing choice, enterprise architects should bucket organizational tasks into distinct operational tiers. Don’t feed every problem into a token-hungry trillion-parameter model if a smaller, specialized one will do the trick.

“Organizations don’t give a heavyweight reasoning model a lightweight sorting job,” said Nutanix’s Dutta. “They divide their business workloads into tiers based on cost, speed and hardware footprint.”.

Lower-tier workloads such as search, embeddings and document classification work well with inexpensive, compact open-weight and small language models. Sophisticated tasks such as autonomous reasoning and restructuring large, deeply entangled legacy software systems are better suited to commercial alternatives.

According to recent reports, ISG’s Bakker believes the need for constant evaluation is the biggest impediment to open-weight adoption. “The core software engineering required to test and integrate new models into the software stack will likely be the biggest hurdle, since not all frontier models have the same capabilities and APIs,” he said. “The frontier labs tend to maintain more consistency in their upgrade paths.”.

Sources indicate that enterprise IT organizations must develop expertise in local model execution, containerized execution sandboxes and agent harness orchestration. Managing AI and agents safely “is, in the near future, going to be as key an indigenous knowledge as how to upgrade Windows,” remarked Gordon Allott, founder and CEO of private infrastructure provider nFOX Lab.

According to recent reports, the shift toward open-weight models represents a permanent maturation of enterprise IT from experimentation to disciplined financial and architectural management. Success is no longer about raw model parameter size or benchmark ranking, but matching the model to the task. That’s a discipline that was barely on the roadmap a year ago.

At the start of the year, there was no way enterprises were going to touch open-weight models, Brad Maltz, head of AI factory solutions at Dell Technologies Inc., said in a November interview on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE’s streaming media platform. “People were pretty wrong about that. I think the open-weight movement is the future.”.

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (564 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housingwire ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Colorado first responders can now get state home mortgage help

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (564 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A borrower earning nearly $197,000 a year usually doesn’t look like a typical candidate for state housing help.
  • The Colorado Housing and Finance Authority rolled out a homeownership program this month for first responders and law enforcement officers.
  • In a recent development, colorado is among a growing list of states offering homebuying assistance to public-service workers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A borrower earning nearly $197,000 a year usually doesn’t look like a typical candidate for state housing help. In Colorado, if that borrower is a firefighter, emergency medical technician or police officer, the person now qualifies.

The Colorado Housing and Finance Authority rolled out a homeownership program this month for first responders and law enforcement officers. CHFA Colorado Champions uses a new state law that raises income limits for eligible borrowers.

In a recent development, colorado is among a growing list of states offering homebuying assistance to public-service workers. The goal is to give them more chances to live near where they serve. Maryland, Tennessee, Oklahoma, Texas, Florida and South Carolina also offer similar programs.

Earlier this month, Connecticut Gov. Ned Lamont unveiled a upcoming homeownership assistance program for first responders. It offers up to $25,000 in forgivable down payment and closing cost assistance. The program stems from a law Lamont signed this year.

“By helping reduce one of the biggest barriers to buying a home, we’re investing in the people who serve our state and the communities that depend on them,” Lamont remarked in a statement.

CHFA Colorado Champions arrives as the housing market weakens, following several years of zoning and regulatory reform.

Colorado’s single-family housing market has been steadily cooling since spring, according to HousingWire Intelligence data through Nov. 20. Inventory peaked in September and has barely eased, while median list prices have fallen since July. Homes are also taking longer to sell, with days on market rising since late July and price reductions staying elevated.

Recent findings suggest that the latest weekly figures show no reversal, with single-family homes taking a median 91 days to sell, up from 84. The median single-family list price is $599,000, and about 48% of single-family listings carry price cuts, the data show.

Recent findings suggest that lawmakers have spent years trying to improve affordability, mostly by loosening local land-use rules. In 2024, Gov. Jared Polis signed laws requiring more density near transit and clearing the way for accessory dwelling units. The package also removed some parking minimums for urban multifamily housing and lifted limits on unrelated people living together.

It has been revealed that A law Polis signed this year requires towns with more than 2,000 people to allow housing on certain small parcels. Eligible land belongs to school districts, colleges, transit districts, housing authorities and qualifying nonprofits. The law takes effect Dec. 31, 2027, while lot-size bills failed in the Legislature this year.

It has been revealed that senate Bill 26-053, a bipartisan law, raised CHFA’s mortgage income limits to 110% of standard guidelines. That allows eligible borrowers earning up to $196,810 a year to qualify.

The program offers a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage. The program covers down payment and closing costs up to the lesser of $25,000 or 4% of the first mortgage. Borrowers apply through a CHFA participating lender.

Sources indicate that the aid is a second mortgage. Repayment is deferred until the term ends, the first mortgage is paid off, or the borrower sells, refinances or moves.

CHFA Executive Director Thomas Bryan stated in a statement that first responders keep communities safe. Many can’t afford local homes, he added.

It has been revealed that “They should be able to live where they serve,” Sen. Barbara Kirkmeyer, one of the law’s sponsors, said in a statement.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housingwire ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Housing data shocks to the upside: Will we get sub-7% rates for Christmas?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (469 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thanksgiving week has been crazy so far, with a stock rally, stocks selling off, the 10-year yield dropping below 4.85%, tariffs being announced, inflation running hot, low jobless claims, strong GDP data and then — the housing data surprised to the upside!
  • Sources indicate that as we’ve discussed in the Housing Market Tracker articles over the past few weeks, our weekly pending sales data has stabilized and last week it grew a bit.
  • Those lower rates stabilized demand in our weekly pending home sales data, which grew last week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thanksgiving week has been crazy so far, with a stock rally, stocks selling off, the 10-year yield dropping below 4.85%, tariffs being announced, inflation running hot, low jobless claims, strong GDP data and then — the housing data surprised to the upside! Let’s look at what’s happening as mortgage rates have fallen a tad from recent highs.

Sources indicate that as we’ve discussed in the Housing Market Tracker articles over the past few weeks, our weekly pending sales data has stabilized and last week it grew a bit. The housing market took a shock when rates rose aggressively from under 7% in September to 7.61% in early October; that shock really impacted demand, but rates haven’t gone higher than that and have eased a bit since.

Those lower rates stabilized demand in our weekly pending home sales data, which grew last week.

Purchase application data, on the other hand, has moved more noticeably. This index can be very tricky at times because it’s a survey, but to see this growth without rates below 7% is a good sign of stabilization.

Of course, the year-over-year purchase application data is still down massive, but last year mortgage rates were roughly 1% lower at this time and we were heading toward a nine-month high in sales last December.

Industry observers note that newly introduced home sales today beat estimates so much that my first inclination was not to believe it! I expect this number will be revised lower, but it’s still a positive trend. New home sales are basically doing the same thing they have done for 10 years, outside the COVID sales burst. They don’t really go below 570,000, nor do they really break away from 730,000. We are stuck in this range, as the builders are still working in a sub-6 % mortgage market, and thus new home sales are still at 2019 levels. If existing home sales were operating at those levels it would amount to 1-1.3 million more existing home sales. However, the existing home market hasn’t had the luxury of sub-6 % mortgage rates.

In a recent development, one positive note that isn’t getting a lot of play is that the builders are slowly moving their completed units of sale lower. If we want housing starts to ever grow again, this needs to happen and fortunately this number has been falling all year long.

As I am writing this article, the 10-year yield is at 4.82%.

If we want sub-7 % rates for Thanksgiving, Christmas, or Upcoming Year’s — as I have written about for weeks — we need the 10-year yield at 4.85% and under. Now, if spreads just improve a little, then we get our sub-7 % mortgage rates for the holidays. It’s been a wild week, folks; enjoy the holiday!

#145044. Sometimes the most valuable data is the house nobody bought

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (815 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Inman ↗ Open Full Page

Sometimes the most valuable data is the house nobody bought

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (815 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that want to price more precisely?
  • Recent findings suggest that when agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds.
  • But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that want to price more precisely? Canceled listing data in the MLS can reveal where buyers stated no. Learn three steps to add failed listings to your next CMA.

Recent findings suggest that when agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds. Look at what’s coming soon, active and pending. Adjust for condition, location, square footage and amenities. Figure out where our house fits.

But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.

Expired. Canceled. Withdrawn. Earlier in my career, I looked at these failed listings all the time. Then the market changed. When inventory became tight, and buyers were competing for homes, digging through failed listings often wasn’t necessary to determine where a property would sell.

Now the market is shifting again; pricing must be more precise, and I’m sharpening my approach by bringing an old tool back into my pricing process.

Industry observers note that A sold comp tells us where a buyer noted yes, but a failed listing can help us figure out where buyers said no. And in a buyer-favored market, that’s valuable information.

Imagine you’re pricing a home, and the recent comparable sales range from $600,000 to $625,000. Then you expand your search.

Suddenly, you know considerably more than the sold comps alone told you. Other sellers have already tested the upper limits of pricing, and buyers responded. It’s essentially a series of pricing experiments someone else conducted for you — and they paid the carrying costs.

Sources indicate that one of the most interesting things buried in MLS history is the pricing journey. A property might show a final list price of $649,000 and an eventual sale of $630,000. Dig deeper, and you may discover this:.

$725,000 → $699,000 → $675,000 → canceled → relisted at $649,000 → sold for $630,000.

That’s a different story. The sale tells us what one buyer eventually paid. The listing history tells us buyers had previously rejected that house at $725,000, $699,000 and $675,000.

It also illustrates something sellers don’t always understand: Getting to the right price eventually isn’t necessarily the same as pricing correctly from the beginning. After months of market exposure and multiple reductions, buyers may stop asking, “Could this be the house?” They start asking, “What’s wrong with it?”.

In a recent development, when I find a comparable property that sat for 90 days without selling, I want to know what did sell during those same 90 days. Sometimes we blame the market when the market was functioning just fine. Buyers were buying houses. They simply weren’t buying that one.

Maybe they chose the renovated house at $640,000. Maybe they paid $650,000 for the better lot. They may have even paid more for another property because it offered something the failed listing didn’t. That’s useful information when you’re sitting across from a seller who believes buyers just need more time to appreciate their home.

If buyers repeatedly toured the property and purchased competing homes instead, the market may already have delivered its opinion.

Sources indicate that this is where agents have to resist oversimplifying the data. An expired listing isn’t automatic proof that a house was overpriced, and a canceled listing certainly isn’t either.

Listings fail for all sorts of reasons. Sellers change their minds. Job transfers fall through. Repairs surface. Agents get fired. Sometimes a seller receives a perfectly acceptable offer and decides not to move.

So, investigate. Call the previous agent. I might simply say:.

Industry observers note that “I’m pricing a similar property and noticed yours was on the market last year. Is there anything you can tell me about the activity or why the seller decided not to continue?”.

According to recent reports, twenty-seven showings and no offers tell me something. Two showings in four months tells me something different.

There’s one more number worth considering: the cost of the pricing journey.

Sources indicate that find a house that started high, sat, reduced, expired, relisted and eventually sold. Then compare it with similar homes that entered the market closer to where buyers were actually buying.

Sellers often view aspirational pricing as a no-risk strategy: “We can always come down.” Technically, that’s true. But time isn’t free, and neither is market perception.

The next time you’re preparing a CMA in a shifting or buyer-favored market:.

We’re very good at studying success in real estate. But as pricing gets harder, I’ve found myself returning to an old habit: studying the failures, too. Sold listings tell us where buyers have been willing to say yes. Sometimes the house nobody bought is the one that tells us exactly where they started saying no.

Roxanne Hale is the associate broker of the Art House Team, brokered by RealtySouth in Birmingham, Alabama. Get connected on Facebook or YouTube.

Industry News: Three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of the Fully Connected event

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1575 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI infrastructure economics are increasingly defined by the cost of producing intelligence rather than acquiring computing capacity.
  • In a recent development, as inference demand outpaces training growth, infrastructure providers and their customers must increase productive computing time without a corresponding rise in operating costs.
  • “What you’re seeing CoreWeave do strategically is they’re expanding out beyond compute,” Vellante stated.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 14:56 EST / NOVEMBER 25 2026.

AI infrastructure economics are increasingly defined by the cost of producing intelligence rather than acquiring computing capacity.

In a recent development, as inference demand outpaces training growth, infrastructure providers and their customers must increase productive computing time without a corresponding rise in operating costs. The emergence of continuously learning agents and physical AI applications is further complicating that equation. For CoreWeave Inc., the changing workload mix is altering the economics of infrastructure delivery, according to theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante and John Furrier.

“What you’re seeing CoreWeave do strategically is they’re expanding out beyond compute,” Vellante stated. “They’ve got networking; they’ve got storage. They’ve got this software layer, which is observability. They’ve got security in there. They’ve got this closed-loop system between evaluation, observation [and] runtime curating … that’s sort of how they’re saying their software layer is now intact.”.

Industry observers note that during the Fully Connected event, Vellante and Furrier spoke with CoreWeave executives, technology partners and customers about the technical and economic realities of running artificial intelligence at production scale. (* Disclosure below.).

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video analysis with Dave Vellante and John Furrier:.

Here are three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s exclusive coverage of this event:.

In a recent development, the commercial value of inference depends on both token volume and delivery speed. Nvidia Corp.’s Groq 3 LPX inference accelerator, which works with its Vera Rubin platform, is attracting interest in financial technology and other sectors that require real-time processing, according to Ian Buck, vice president and general manager of hyperscale and HPC at Nvidia.

“Data centers have a natural cap, and that cap is actually their power,” he told theCUBE. “With every generation of GPU, we make sure that our tokens per watt is upwards of 10 times more efficient. In fact, we saw that with Blackwell — we got, in the end, a 30x improvement in tokens per watt.”.

In a recent development, memory management adds another dimension to AI infrastructure economics as agents engage in increasingly lengthy interactions. A single session involving 500,000 tokens can consume between 5% and 10% of a graphics processing unit’s memory. Retaining session context in persistent storage can reduce costly recalculations, according to Alon Horev, co-founder and chief technology officer of Vast Data Inc.

Industry observers note that “You can move a session from one busy GPU to one less busy GPU and move KV cache either over the network or read it from Vast,” he told theCUBE. “Once you look at inference as a distributed problem where you have the opportunity to use GPU memory, CPU memory and Vast across a fleet of machines, you have more optionality and you have more optimized scheduling.”.

For AI-native startups, specialized cloud providers offer an alternative to owning capital-intensive infrastructure. LlamaIndex Inc. processes millions of document pages daily for customers in finance, legal services and insurance. Inference accounts for about 75% of its workloads, with training accounting for the remainder, according to Jerry Liu, co-founder and chief executive officer of LlamaIndex.

Sources indicate that “We serve a lot of different customers at extremely persistent and also spiky workloads,” he told theCUBE. “We really, really need to make sure that we have the right capacity to serve our customers without getting throttled.”.

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Ian Buck:.

According to recent reports, protecting AI infrastructure investments starts on the factory floor. Dell Technologies Inc. has developed modular rack designs to accommodate different power and cooling configurations. Its collaboration with CoreWeave includes integrating the cloud provider’s Racky management software into factory testing and improving liquid-cooling leak detection, according to Sarat Krishnan, director of PowerEdge AI architecture and systems development engineering at Dell.

Industry observers note that “It becomes increasingly expensive to remediate and fix something as you go later on in the manufacturing process; [it] becomes extremely expensive if you have to replace something in the data center,” he told theCUBE. “What we have done over the last two years is shift our most complex diagnostics — the ones that are going to capture true hardware failures — further and further left.”.

At Cognition AI Inc., continuous model improvement involves training across data centers in multiple countries. The organization’s Devin software engineering agent now handles tasks ranging from code development to resolving production complications, according to Chen Goldberg (pictured, left), executive vice president of product and engineering at CoreWeave, and Silas Alberti (right), head of research and founding team at Cognition. To support these learning systems, CoreWeave introduced Forge, a platform that connects inference, evaluation and model refinement and incorporates Agent Lens to trace agent activity.

In a recent development, “If you run a big training run, you’re not just looking at the GPUs, but you also want uptime,” Alberti noted during the event. “If just one replica goes down, the whole training run goes down. I think a very important metric is getting to this 99.99% reliability.”.

Industry observers note that for International Business Machines Corp., the power and cooling demands of newer hardware helped drive its decision to work with CoreWeave. The relationship has since expanded to include joint engineering around identity management and workload isolation through CoreWeave Sandboxes. IBM also benchmarks the performance impact of security controls to inform architectural decisions, according to Brian Belgodere, senior technical staff member at IBM.

Industry observers note that “This is a supply chain problem, top to bottom,” Belgodere told theCUBE. “It’s not just the hardware: it’s the firmware, kernel levels, code, your data provenance. Then you get into the whole world of agents, your images. It is an absolute provenance problem.”.

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Brian Belgodere:.

For organizations deploying physical AI, implementation time is a key consideration in AI infrastructure economics. Aston Martin F1, whose race cars generate a million data points per second each, operates under strict budget constraints and development deadlines. CoreWeave’s forward-deployed engineering approach brings specialized expertise to those operations, according to Richard Ahlfeld, senior vice president of physical AI at CoreWeave, and Eric Ernst, commercial technology ambassador of AMR GP Ltd., trading as Aston Martin F1.

In a recent development, “We really need people that can be outside of the car development phase and come in with the fresh knowledge of what’s happening in this industry that is moving extremely quickly,” Ernst said during the event. “You can build as many processes as you want, call it agile, whatever you want. You cannot stop that process. You got to hit a deadline.”.

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Richard Ahlfeld and Eric Ernst:.

Recent findings suggest that walden Robotics Inc. uses large-scale virtual simulation to prepare robots for physical deployment. Its robots have been working full production shifts alongside humans since May, performing tasks such as machine tending, parts kitting and subassembly, according to Adrien Gaidon, co-founder and chief strategy officer of Walden Robotics, and John Mancuso, vice president of field engineering at CoreWeave Inc.

“If you’re changing things and you have machines that cannot change and continuously learn in deployment, then you become a burden,” Gaidon told theCUBE. “We do machines that continuously learn from deployment and adapt so customers can change their mind and improve the process and give them the superpower to change even more and faster.”.

Here’s theCUBE’s full video discussion with John Mancuso and Adrien Gaidon:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

Industry observers note that ripple’s dollar-pegged stablecoin, Ripple USD (RLUSD), has now entered the top five stablecoins by market cap, reaching a fresh all-time high in its circulating supply, a major milestone for the stablecoin less than two years after its launch. RLUSD went live in December 2024.

In a recent development, RLUSD has surpassed World Liberty Financial USD (USD1), Global Dollar (USDG) and PayPal USD (PYUSD) to become the fifth-largest stablecoin in the world, according to data from CoinMarketCap. Only Tether’s USDT, Circle’s USDC, Ethena’s USDe, and Dai (DAI) are ahead of it.

The milestone is proof of the rapid growth RLUSD has experienced in a competitive stablecoin market dominated by established players like Tether’s USDT and Circle’s USDC.

RLUSD’s total circulating supply across the XRP Ledger and Ethereum has reached a new high, with $2.85 billion in circulation, according to Ripple’s stablecoin tracker.

Ethereum commands $2.089 billion of this total figure, while $768 million in supply sits on the XRP Ledger. While Ethereum currently holds the larger share of RLUSD’s supply, XRPL has seen significant activity in RLUSD settlement volumes.

In March 2025, during a Bloomberg TV interview, Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse projected that RLUSD would enter the top five stablecoins; that projection has now been fulfilled.

According to RWA Foundation, Ripple led weekly stablecoin growth, adding $75.4 million in the last seven days. This growth was reflected in RLUSD's market cap, allowing it to surpass World Liberty Financial USD to clinch the fifth spot in global stablecoin rankings.

Former Ripple executive Anthony Welfare highlighted this growth in a recent X post, saying, “RLUSD is the only major stablecoin growing right now.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Connecticut is the latest state to help first responders reach their homeownership goals with assistance for down payments and closing costs.
  • In a recent development, the “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing.
  • In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Connecticut is the latest state to help first responders reach their homeownership goals with assistance for down payments and closing costs.

In a recent development, the “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing. To qualify, first responders must have completed two years of service and purchase a primary residence within the community they serve.

In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.

“Connecticut’s police officers, firefighters and EMS personnel dedicate themselves to protecting our families and communities, and we want to make sure they have the opportunity to build their own futures here,” Governor Ned Lamont remarked in a prepared statement on Tuesday. “By helping reduce one of the biggest barriers to buying a home, we’re investing in the people who serve our state and the communities that depend on them.”.

The program is part of Public Act 26-12, a state bill that aims to increase the number of first responders with a number of incentives, including college tuition reimbursement and improved labor protections.

“The people who protect and serve our communities should be able to afford to live in those communities, and this program with help them do it,” Comptroller Sean Scanlon remarked in a written statement. “Helping the people who put their lives on the line for us every day buy their first home is literally the least we can do, and I’m proud to have worked with Governor Lamont and legislature to make this a reality.”.

It has been revealed that seven other states also have down payment assistance programs for first responders. Florida, Nevada, Georgia and South Carolina provide flat amounts, ranging from $10,000 to $35,000. Texas, Maryland and Ohio’s programs are percentage-based and offer assistance ranging from 2.5 percent to 5 percent of the purchase price.

The terms of each program vary. Most states forgive the assistance after five to seven years, but Nevada requires homebuyers to repay the funds within 30 years. And like Connecticut, Ohio also offers a 0.25 percent mortgage rate discount.

“Homeownership offers more than a place to live. It creates stability, strengthens connections to community and provides an opportunity to build wealth over time,” CHFA CEO and Executive Director Nandini Natarajan noted in an announcement. “Through First Responders’ Time to Own, we’re helping the people who answer the call for our communities take an crucial step toward achieving their own homeownership goals.”.

First responders often fall through the cracks of housing assistance programs because they don’t earn enough to afford market-rate housing but earn too much to qualify for federal housing vouchers.

Inman explored this dilemma last September in a feature on workforce housing in resort towns like Jackson Hole, Vail and Tahoe. These towns can’t operate without first responders and other essential workers in the hospitality and retail sectors. However, rental and for-sale home prices have far outpaced what these workers earn, forcing them to commute long distances from more affordable towns or take on second and third jobs to survive.

The solution for some of these towns has been investing in workforce housing, which caps prices for households that earn between 60 percent and 120 percent of their area’s AMI. Most workforce housing is rent-only, but some states are extending the programs to include for-sale properties.

It has been revealed that “I think the fact that workforce housing can be necessary or is a thing in the first place is really an indictment of the state of housing affordability in the country today,” Realtor.com Senior Economist Jake Krimmel noted. “I think it’s key to ground any conversation about workforce and affordable housing in that reality. It’s a market failure and a policy failure that someone could be a doctor, a teacher or another kind of professional and cannot afford to pay the market rent or own a home outright.”.

Windermere Principal Economist Jeff Tucker said workforce housing isn’t a panacea for affordability and works within an ecosystem of other housing and economic policies, such as upzoning, to create a more equitable market.

Tucker’s comments came a month after the Senate introduced the ROAD to Housing Act of 2025, and three months before the House introduced the Housing for the 21st Century Act. The bills were eventually combined into the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which passed in June.

In a recent development, “A broad package of necessary reforms to make more housing construction possible in much of the country is a really vital component of a long-term solution to the housing affordability challenges we face,” Tucker said. “Our current housing shortage took years to develop. So it’ll take years to build our way out of it.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, fresh home sales blipped above expectations in October, handing homebuilders a slice of better-than-worse, Thanksgiving-time, good news. However, NAHB’s November homebuilder confidence gauge had plunged to its lowest level in nearly 15 years, signaling that builders remain pessimistic about the market’s current state and foreseeable-future direction.

According to recent reports, according to U.S. Census Bureau data, sales of newly constructed single-family homes in October came in at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 701,000, up 14.2% month-over month, and a 7.5% gain from the same month a year prior. Meanwhile, the median sales price of fresh homes sold in October was $391,000, down 0.3% from September and 3.2% from a year ago.

In a recent development, october’s better-than-forecast results may surprise many, but they come with a catch: the survey’s margin of error and data collection cycle. They could be revised downward next month.

“A downward revision to September helps explain the size of October’s 14.2% rebound, the largest monthly gain since November 2025,” First American Deputy Chief Economist Odeta Kushi noted in a statement.

New home for-sale inventory also tightened, coinciding with a decline in new residential construction. The seasonally adjusted estimate of new homes for sale at the end of October was 470,000, down 1.5% from September’s 477,000, and 4.1% below the 490,000 recorded in October 2025. At the current sales rate, that represents a supply of 8.0 months, a 14% improvement from 9.3 months in September and 11.1% from 9.0 months a year earlier.

October’s sales results may be less of a bright spot than they appear, and one strong month doesn’t erase the warning signs flashing across the new home market.

Plenty of indications suggest homebuilders are working through one of the toughest housing markets in years, including homebuilder confidence at its lowest point since the tail end of the Great Financial Crisis.

For example, mortgage applications for new-home purchases fell 13.6% year over year in October, a sign that rising mortgage rates and low consumer confidence continue to weigh on demand. The existing-home market is also struggling, with the National Association of Realtors reporting that pending home sales fell to another record low in October.

NAHB also reports that, in November, homebuilders had a bleak view of current sales conditions, future sales expectations for the next six months and prospective buyer traffic.

“Persistent housing affordability challenges, including elevated home prices and mortgage rates, continue to weigh on prospective buyers and constrain demand,” Danushka Nanayakkara-Skillington, NAHB Assistant VP for Forecasting and Analysis, wrote in a note following today’s upcoming home sales release. “Builders are using sales incentives and price adjustments to attract buyers, but affordability remains a significant obstacle to a sustained recovery in housing demand.”.

A review of the latest earnings calls from 14 publicly traded homebuilders reveals that the country’s largest builders faced a challenging third quarter, with sales conditions remaining weak heading into the final months of the year, consistent with NAHB’s data.

Last quarter, only three of the public homebuilders — Smith Douglas Homes, Toll Brothers and Green Brick Partners — reported year-over-year increases in fresh orders. However, nearly all 14 experienced sequential declines in orders, many exceeding 20%, pointing to a further deterioration in demand.

Industry observers note that sales volume followed a similar trend. Only Smith Douglas Homes and LGI Homes reported year-over-year increases in homes sold,.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, just two builders, Toll Brothers (2.4%) and Hovnanian Enterprises (0.4%), posted year-over-year increases in average sales prices. Toll’s luxury-focused buyer base is generally less sensitive to mortgage rates and economic volatility, while Hovnanian has increasingly shifted its product mix toward move-up and active-adult buyers, who tend to be more resilient to broader market pressures.

Many public homebuilders reported in October and November that buyers remain very cautious, which helped dampen sales volume and prices.

“As we moved through the quarter, our buyers became more cautious, did not feel an urgency to transact and felt more comfortable moving to the sidelines,” Century Communities Executive Chairman Dale Francescon said during an earnings call on October 28.

Paul Romanowski, President and CEO at D.R. Horton, acknowledged that October was another challenging month.

It has been revealed that “Demand did get weaker as the quarter went on, for sure. As rates rose and as we got into October, what we’ve seen mirrors September. Traffic and sales activity are somewhat below what we’d anticipate in a typical seasonal pattern,” he said during an earnings call on October 29.

Against this backdrop, it remains unclear whether October’s sales rebound reflects a meaningful improvement in demand or a temporary spike that could show up next month as a downward revision.

In a recent development, “Looking ahead, the question is whether enough buyers will follow those who signed contracts in October,” Kushi mentioned, pointing to falling mortgage applications for upcoming homes and low homebuilder confidence. “Builders are finding ways to make the monthly payment work for some buyers, but softer buyer traffic and fewer mortgage applications point to a tough winter.”.

Bitcoin (BTC) fell as low as $55,081 on Nov. 21, its lowest price since September 2024, according to TradingView data. The cryptocurrency then bounced back and was trading at $60,583 on Sunday, after it opened November at $77,425.

Bitcoin has lost 21.6% so far in November 2026, according to CryptoRank. The last time Bitcoin had a worse month was June 2022, when the cryptocurrency lost 37.9%, according to the same data.

It has been revealed that the four-year cycle theory ties Bitcoin's market cycles to halvings, and its supporters point to 2014, 2018 and 2022 as the years when each bear market went through its final sell-off. In this context, 2026 is the next year in that row, and the next Bitcoin halving is expected in April 2028. The previous three halvings took place in July 2016, May 2020 and April 2024.

In a recent development, bitcoin set its record above $1,100 in late 2013. In February 2014, the Japanese exchange Mt. Gox, which handled most Bitcoin trading in 2013, filed for bankruptcy after it lost about 850,000 BTC. In November 2014, Bitcoin gained 11.6%, according to CryptoRank, but December of that year brought a 15.3% drop, and the bottom below $200 came in January 2015.

In December 2017, Bitcoin reached a record near $20,000 on the back of the ICO boom, and during 2018, the ICO market dried up. In November 2018, the crypto market crashed after the Bitcoin Cash hard fork and the so-called hash war between the two camps of miners, and Bitcoin lost 36.4% that month. The cryptocurrency then lost another 6.4% in December 2018 and set its cycle low at about $3,200 in the middle of that month.

The 2021 record near $69,000 came in November 2021. In May 2022, the Terra ecosystem collapsed, and in July of that year, Celsius and Three Arrows Capital filed for bankruptcy. In November of that year, the FTX exchange went bankrupt. Bitcoin lost 16.1% in November 2022 and set its bear market bottom at around $15,500 on Nov. 21, 2022, four years to the day before the latest low. December of that year brought a 3.7% loss, and in January 2023, Bitcoin gained 39.9%.

In the current cycle, Bitcoin set its record above $126,000 in October 2025. In 2026, Bitcoin has lost value in six of the 11 months so far, according to CryptoRank. On Nov. 20, the cryptocurrency fell below $60,000 for the first time since July, and the decline continued the next day.

The latest drop comes amid a broad sell-off on Wall Street, where technology and AI stocks came under pressure, and amid expectations of further interest-rate hikes by the Federal Reserve.

Micron Inc., one of the world’s top memory chip suppliers, saw its market capitalization drop more than 4.5% today. Oracle Corp., which trails the three companies in market share but has emerged as an notable AI infrastructure provider, took the biggest hit: It’s down 5% from yesterday.

Industry observers note that anthropic ended the trading session with a 1% gain. The company thereby recouped some of yesterday’s losses, which pushed its stock below its $80 debut price. Anthropic went public last week through a record-setting offering that raised more than $93 billion.

Overall, the tech-heavy Nasdaq lost 0.6% while the S&P 500 slid 0.25%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 0.33%.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Famous Bitcoin (BTC) advocate and investor Bill Miller IV said that it is much easier to value the world's largest cryptocurrency than AI investments, even though Bitcoin does not produce any cash flow.
  • He noted that this has to do with the expectations investors have when it comes to these two assets, specifically regarding their capacity to deliver future profits.
  • In a recent X post, Miller, who is the chairman and chief investment officer of Miller Value Partners, broke down why he thinks that it's easier to make an investment case for Bitcoin than for AI companies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Famous Bitcoin (BTC) advocate and investor Bill Miller IV said that it is much easier to value the world's largest cryptocurrency than AI investments, even though Bitcoin does not produce any cash flow.

He noted that this has to do with the expectations investors have when it comes to these two assets, specifically regarding their capacity to deliver future profits.

In a recent X post, Miller, who is the chairman and chief investment officer of Miller Value Partners, broke down why he thinks that it's easier to make an investment case for Bitcoin than for AI companies.

In a recent development, "Bitcoin and AI owners have different expectations. The owners of AI expect companies will one day produce free cash flow. Bitcoin owners never did or will expect this," Miller stated.

And the end result is that "the valuation case is still much easier for Bitcoin than AI.".

Simply put, when investors buy stocks in AI companies, there is an expectation that at some point these companies will deliver significant profits and free cash flow.

Free cash flow is the money a company produces from its operations after capital expenditures. This is a significant metric for understanding the value of a company.

However, when it comes to AI companies, it can be difficult to assign a value because investors need to try to determine what kind of revenue these companies will generate, how much they will invest in infrastructure, and when these investments will start to deliver sufficient returns.

Miller has made it a point to push back against the argument that Bitcoin does not have value because it doesn't produce cash flow.

In a commentary from June 30, Miller explained that the traditional way of looking at intrinsic value, which revolves around future cash flows, doesn't really capture the potential of Bitcoin as a decentralized monetary network.

Instead, Miller said that Bitcoin's value could be determined by comparing its potential role within the global financial system to that of gold.

In his view, Bitcoin could theoretically reach about $1.4 million per coin if it achieved a valuation similar to gold's. At least, that's what he calculated at the time.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • On Thanksgiving eve, Judge Brendan Lantry dismissed a landlords’ challenge to the Rent Guidelines Board’s late June decision to freeze rents.
  • With the national real estate industry watching, the rent freeze became a major test of what a mayor can do to force affordability.
  • Recent findings suggest that owners of rent-stabilized buildings argued that Mamdani stacked the board with loyalists after promising a freeze, making the outcome predetermined.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Thanksgiving eve, Judge Brendan Lantry dismissed a landlords’ challenge to the Rent Guidelines Board’s late June decision to freeze rents. The ruling upholds the city’s first-ever freeze on both one- and two-year leases.

With the national real estate industry watching, the rent freeze became a major test of what a mayor can do to force affordability.

Recent findings suggest that owners of rent-stabilized buildings argued that Mamdani stacked the board with loyalists after promising a freeze, making the outcome predetermined. They also accused the board of following a campaign promise instead of the data on rising landlord costs. Lantry rejected both claims.

In a recent development, the ruling comes three weeks after an appeals court revived the city’s pied-à-terre tax rollout on second homes valued at $5 million or higher. Mamdani posted on social media that the city has billed owners of those homes more than $500 million.

In a recent development, that lawsuit ran parallel to the rent freeze lawsuit landlords filed in late July. It originally was in a Staten Island court but was moved to Manhattan in August at the city’s request.

Sources indicate that the rent freeze took effect Oct. 1 while the lawsuit was pending and covers leases on more than a million apartments. The board had frozen one-year leases in 2015, 2016 and 2020.

According to recent reports, because the board acts in a quasi-legislative role, its orders stand if they have a rational basis, and courts may not substitute their own judgment, Lantry wrote. He found that the board’s 42-page explanatory statement showed it considered each factor the Administrative Code requires, including the industry’s economic condition and the cost of living.

It has been revealed that lantry stated appointees who share the mayor’s views did not show collusion. He noted that “elections have consequences.”.

But Lantry did not let Mamdani completely off the hook.

“Regarding Mayor Mamdani’s campaign for Mayor of New York City, the court would be remiss not to state that such comments, promises, and guarantees to freeze the rent were reckless and irresponsible,” he wrote. “The Mayor of the City of New York has no authority to unilaterally raise, ‘freeze’ or otherwise adjust the rent of stabilized units in this City – that responsibility is within the power of the Board and the Board alone.”.

Industry observers note that he called an email in which the board’s chair shared a draft of the explanatory statement with a mayoral aide before the vote “troubling.” He said it cast a “dark shadow” over the board’s independence. Without more, he wrote, the email did not justify overturning the decision under Article 78, the state law that lets courts review government agency actions.

The judge noted that petitioners agreed to end court-ordered discovery, which produced about 1,000 documents, and never sought depositions.

Lantry acknowledged the freeze could make it harder for owners to refinance or renovate. But he wrote that the legal question is not whether the policy is wise.

  • A “Saturday Night Live” skit about caring for aging relatives touched a viral nerve after it aired over the weekend, including with Melinda French Gates, who offered her own “fact check” on the too-close-to-home comedy.
  • The sketch, a fake commercial, stars host John Mulaney as a man who has found an easy way to care for his aging father without upending his own life: “Sister,” an “elder care system” that is free and is, in fact, his sister.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 1:23 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 1:23 pm.

A “Saturday Night Live” skit about caring for aging relatives touched a viral nerve after it aired over the weekend, including with Melinda French Gates, who offered her own “fact check” on the too-close-to-home comedy.

The sketch, a fake commercial, stars host John Mulaney as a man who has found an easy way to care for his aging father without upending his own life: “Sister,” an “elder care system” that is free and is, in fact, his sister.

French Gates wrote on Instagram this week that the sketch “is funny because it’s a little too true.” Using research from Pivotal, her investment and philanthropic organization, she went through the ad’s claims one by one and found that most held up:.

In a recent development, sister will provide. True, French Gates mentioned, citing AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving. Among adults ages 55 to 64, women are nearly 40% more likely than men to care for an older relative, and nearly 40% more likely to provide constant care.

Sources indicate that she’ll quit her job. “Mostly true,” at least the job part. Catalyst found that 42% of women who voluntarily left jobs in 2025 cited caregiving as the main reason.

According to recent reports, paid help is pricey. “True, unfortunately.” New America puts the average home health aide at more than $6,600 a month, and 24-hour care can top $25,000.

Sources indicate that sister may break down. Also true. In the Caregiving in the U.S. 2025 report, nearly two-thirds of caregivers said they were under moderate or high emotional stress, and women felt the strain more than men did.

Industry observers note that “Free” is misleading. French Gates said Sister isn’t free; she’s the one paying for the care, in lost wages, stalled careers, thinner retirement savings and less time for her own life.

French Gates has made women’s health and caregiving central to her work since she stepped down as co-chair of the Gates Foundation in 2024.

Recent findings suggest that she left with $12.5 billion to put toward her work on behalf of women and families. Much of that work runs through Pivotal, the Seattle-area organization she founded to handle her philanthropy and investments. In June she pledged another $215 million for women’s health, which brought her giving in that area to more than $600 million over two years. The pledge included $10 million to the Menopause Society for better menopause care in the U.S.

The sketch has been shared widely across the country this week, in part because it lines up so closely with the research.

In its own analysis, The Fresh York Times cited studies showing that daughters generally provide at least twice as much care to aging parents as sons do. The U.S., unlike many wealthy countries, offers no federal paid leave or long-term care insurance for family caregivers.

French Gates noted she welcomed the conversation.

“I’m so glad we’re talking about this, and laughing about it,” she wrote on Instagram. “We need more honesty about what caring for loved ones really takes and why so much of that work falls to women. But I’d love for the day to come when these jokes don’t pack quite the same punch — because we’ve made it so much easier to care for the people we love.”.

Latest Update: Attacker used 1Password employee’s GitHub account to copy customer records

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (903 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Identity security firm 1Password today disclosed a security incident in which an attacker, working through an employee’s corporate GitHub account, copied account records belonging to a subset of its customers.
  • It has been revealed that according to the organization, the incident came to light on Nov.
  • In a recent development, the records taken include names and email addresses, account and user identifiers, account creation and last sign-in times, public keys, Secure Remote Password protocol parameters and other non-secret account metadata.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 17:29 EST / NOVEMBER 25 2026.

Identity security firm 1Password today disclosed a security incident in which an attacker, working through an employee’s corporate GitHub account, copied account records belonging to a subset of its customers.

It has been revealed that according to the organization, the incident came to light on Nov. 19, when 1Password began investigating signs that the GitHub account had been compromised. Using the account, the attacker is stated to have pushed malicious code to 1Password’s backend services, which then downloaded what the company describes as “administrative data pertaining to our customers.”.

In a recent development, the records taken include names and email addresses, account and user identifiers, account creation and last sign-in times, public keys, Secure Remote Password protocol parameters and other non-secret account metadata. Rounding out the list are tokens found in certain emailed links for invitations, provisioning and account recovery.

Customer vaults, the items stored in them and the keys that protect them were not affected, according to 1Password. “At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker,” the company noted in its disclosure. Account passwords and Secret Keys are not stored by the company. Also left untouched, the company claims, were account recovery keys and the 1Password apps and browser extensions.

Sources indicate that beyond the customer records, the attacker is said to have copied source code from private repositories. Access was also gained to 1Password’s continuous integration and continuous delivery system, which contains infrastructure-related secrets needed for its product to work. According to 1Password, the source code contains no user secrets. Having triggered a rotation of all credentials that may have been exposed, the manufacturer claims there has been no impact to its services, availability or product security.

The tokens taken from emailed links cannot be used on their own to access an account, since completing an invitation or recovery also requires a sign-in through single sign-on or a six-digit code sent to the user’s registered email address. Owners with provisioning invites or recovery requests pending at the time of the incident, mentioned to be a small number, have been notified directly.

As a precaution, the emailed codes have now been lengthened from six numeric digits to 10 alphanumeric characters. 1Password says it has found no internal evidence of account takeovers using the exposed tokens. Other steps taken in response include disabling the affected GitHub account, revoking the stolen token, tightening internal controls and bringing in independent cybersecurity experts to validate its containment and remediation work.

According to recent reports, customers do not need to change anything in their 1Password accounts. The manufacturer is instead warning owners to be cautious of phishing attempts, such as unexpected emails, texts or calls about invitations or account recovery requests they did not start. “1Password will never contact you to ask for your account password or Secret Key,” the company noted.

1Password, which claims to serve more than 200,000 businesses, did not say how many customers had records downloaded. How the employee’s GitHub account was compromised was also left unexplained.

This is not the first intrusion 1Password has disclosed. In October 2023, the tech giant stated that an attacker had accessed its Okta tenant using session data stolen in the breach of Okta Inc.’s customer support system. No user data was found to have been compromised in that case.

Today’s disclosure comes nearly four years after rival password manager LastPass US LP revealed that a hacker had copied encrypted customer password vaults, using information taken in an earlier breach of its development environment.

1Password states it will enhancement its post if the investigation turns up anything that changes what it has disclosed so far.
