Tech Report: From Mamdani to mass-scale empathy: Mast CEO Grant Canary’s unexpected take on climate action

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1112 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 23, 2026 at 8:00 amNovember 23, 2026 at 2:28 pm.
  • Since Grant Canary launched his organization a decade ago, the technology he uses has shifted and pivoted but the goal has remained steadfast: restoring wild forestland.
  • The Seattle startup began as DroneSeed, which mapped forests devastated by fires, then flew large drones to re-tree the landscape.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 23, 2026 at 8:00 amNovember 23, 2026 at 2:28 pm.

Since Grant Canary launched his organization a decade ago, the technology he uses has shifted and pivoted but the goal has remained steadfast: restoring wild forestland.

The Seattle startup began as DroneSeed, which mapped forests devastated by fires, then flew large drones to re-tree the landscape. It went on to purchase three companies that collect and cultivate conifer seeds and grow saplings for planting, and rebranded as Mast Reforestation.

Sources indicate that the firm recently shifted again, adding a fresh line of operations: taking scorched timber and burying it in clay-lined vaults where it won’t rot and release carbon. Biomass burial clears the woody debris — the most expensive step in forest restoration post wildfire — while also generating essential revenue by selling carbon credits. Proceeds from the sales help landowners “get their forest back,” Canary remarked, which benefits everyone.

Just as Canary has pursued unexpected paths to forest restoration, the sustainability leader also has unconventional solutions and sources of inspiration for tackling climate change. Keep reading to learn more. His quotes have been edited for clarity and length.

When did you realize you had to work in sustainability?

High school. I had a really fantastic teacher my senior year, and they got me focused on my philosophical underpinnings. I’m a utilitarian — greatest good for the greatest number of people, is how I would define that — and so my worldview formed around that time. And climate change is the problem that all other problems report to.

What’s your biggest worry when it comes to solving climate change?

In a recent development, humans aren’t great at long-term projection. We’re much more responsive to short-term, and I am concerned that by the time that it is short-term, which is now, that there is not enough political will to understand the implications of climate change and how that affects all of the concerns.

What gives you the most hope for the planet?

When I founded what would become Mast, there were not the technologies to replace the [fossil fuel] incumbents. That was 2016. The state of EVs versus internal combustion engine cars was not there yet. It’s getting there quickly. Solar was not necessarily the cheapest. Battery was still not there. Geothermal, we didn’t have that. Now we continue to have more and more of those tools to replace the incumbents. And by the way, the “incumbents” is the corporation, not the people working for those companies.

Sources indicate that I very much want all of the better products and technologies. Yes, they’re sustainable, but they’re also just better. I want to brain drain all of the oil and gas companies and put them to work in geothermal.

If you could invent one sustainability solution overnight, what would it be?

In “Ready Player Two” [a sequel to “Ready Player One,” which Steven Spielberg turned into a movie], there is a technology that allows you to step into other humans’ lived experience and feel — and not just in video form, but in the smells, in the emotions, in the feelings, and basically live out other people’s lived experience.

In a recent development, that ability to make empathy mass scale would be a massive game changer in humans having more empathy for each other and understanding the challenges and problems that others are dealing with globally. That would be the technology that would advance things significantly.

What’s one habit you’ve changed personally because of environmental concerns?

In a recent development, my personal infrastructure. I’m lucky enough to have bought a house a few years ago and upgraded to a heat pump; Span [electrical] panels, which sets us up for vehicle-to-grid, solar, batteries, other things; an EV; and then less glamorous but equally notable: insulation, both in the siding and in the windows and blinds. I’m sort of on my journey. We already have an electric cooktop, it’s not the amazing kind, and we have gas hot water heaters, so those are next up — and solar and batteries.

Coffee with any sustainability leader, past or present — who do you pick?

I would change the question and say, who would I want to work for? There’s a ton to learn from someone by working for them, and I think my answer then is [New York City Mayor Zohran] Mamdani. Not a sustainability leader by default, but he has accomplished and built a political backing to do massive things that are ambitious, and from a sustainability lens, I would want to learn from that.

It has been revealed that in the climate space, when we got started, the problem was [a need for more sustainable] tools. It has moved down the supply chain into execution, it’s go-to-market, and that means political will.

What’s the most overhyped climate solution right now?

AI. I use it. I enjoy it. I think it’s fun. But to say that it will solve the challenges of climate in the future are complete red herrings. AI is available to both sides. It is equally as effective at making gas extraction, oil extraction cheaper, faster, etc. as it is helping sustainable technologies get off the ground, and so I would say it is a neutral technology at best.

What’s an underrated solution that deserves more attention?

Nature as infrastructure. If people can’t get themselves to the place where they value forests for their aesthetics, for the health, for the community, for all of the other things, fine. Look at it on a spreadsheet and tell me how much it’s going to cost to replace several hundred thousand acres of forest with water treatment plants, water chiller plants, water purification plants, because that’s going to be a lot of tax dollars. And if we just let it burn, if we clear-cut it all to oblivion, that means that the city of Seattle’s water supply is not going to be as cold. It’s going to require a hell of a lot more purification, and there’s not going to be as much of it.

What impact do you hope your work has in 20 years?

Sources indicate that my hope is that we’ve established the funding source for reforestation with a carbon market. The carbon market is what pulls nature as infrastructure into a valued asset. It’s not an esoteric nice-to-have from a philosophical perspective, it is a valued asset that puts it into the human system of economics in a much bigger way. A carbon market is as substantial an evolutionary step for humanity as the printing press, as banking, as generally accepted accounting principles.

#144928. Why businesses are embracing ‘good enough’ open-weight AI—and how geopolitics could get in the way

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1409 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fortune ↗ Open Full Page

Why businesses are embracing ‘good enough’ open-weight AI—and how geopolitics could get in the way

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1409 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As the performance gap between open-weight and closed-weight models narrows, a growing number of businesses—from local start-ups to large multinationals—are turning to open-weight models for greater control, customization and cost efficiency.
  • Recent findings suggest that “Frontier models at scale are incredibly expensive,” Damian Kim, the Asia-Pacific vice president of visual search and shopping platform Pinterest, tells Fortune.
  • It has been revealed that anyone can download and customize the weights behind an open-weight model, which means firms can cut token costs while keeping tighter control of their data.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As the performance gap between open-weight and closed-weight models narrows, a growing number of businesses—from local start-ups to large multinationals—are turning to open-weight models for greater control, customization and cost efficiency.

Recent findings suggest that “Frontier models at scale are incredibly expensive,” Damian Kim, the Asia-Pacific vice president of visual search and shopping platform Pinterest, tells Fortune. “The cost to serve can be reduced dramatically when using an open-weight model versus a frontier model, where you’re at the whims of the API pricing.”.

It has been revealed that anyone can download and customize the weights behind an open-weight model, which means firms can cut token costs while keeping tighter control of their data. They’re also taking a growing share of AI traffic. In August, open-weight models ran the majority of traffic on Vercel’s AI gateway; 56% of tokens routed through the cloud platform went to open-weight models, up from 7% last year.

“Models are converging on similar performance for industry use: U.S. government evaluators put the best Chinese model about eight months behind the American frontier,” says Olaf Groth, a professor of practice at UC Berkeley’s Haas School of Business. “For most enterprise workloads, that is good enough.”.

According to recent reports, rather than paying for the most powerful model for every task, companies are turning to cheaper, customizable alternatives for routine work. But with Chinese developers behind many of the leading open-weight models, geopolitics may matter as much as cost or performance.

In a recent development, before GPT-3.5 propelled AI to mainstream fame, most high-performing models were either small academic releases or commercial systems with restricted outside access. The first open-weight models originated in academic research, where sharing model weights to ensure reproducibility was standard practice.

Industry observers note that in 2019, OpenAI went against tradition by initially withholding the full 1.5-billion-parameter version of GPT-2, citing risks of misuse such as disinformation, impersonation and phishing. Most U.S. frontier labs, including Anthropic and OpenAI, keep the underlying parameters private, giving owners access through apps or APIs rather than letting them download and run the models themselves.

In the early years of generative AI, most consumers preferred closed-weight models because they delivered performance that open-weight alternatives could not match. Yet in recent years, the improved capability and cost-efficiency of powerful Chinese models like Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3.1 Pro and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash has swung the pendulum back in favor of open-weight models.

It has been revealed that “For the longest time, the idea has been that you can get the highest level of performance using closed-weight models, so many firms start off by using them,” says Hariharasudhan Saminathan, cofounder of Friday, a sovereign AI startup backed by global venture capital firm Antler. But now, “through distillation and other processes, open-weight models’ performance almost matches that of closed-weight models,” he says.

According to recent reports, “Many of our pipeline customers are now adopting open-weight models right off the bat,” he adds. “They’re not even touching the closed-weight ones.”.

Pinterest, for example, uses Alibaba’s open-weight Qwen models to power its online platform. “We’ve driven down our inference costs using post-trained open-weight models,” Kim explains. “They offer over 90% cost reduction.” (Many leading Chinese open-weight models activate only a subset of parameters per token, cutting compute and energy needed per request.).

Kim also cites the flexibility of these models as a draw. Last October, the firm released Pinterest Assistant: an AI-powered tool that pairs a customized Qwen multimodal LLM with the firm’s proprietary Taste Graph, to generate shopping recommendations for customers based on their individual aesthetic preferences.

“[With open-weight technology], we can create a specialized model that actually does what we need it to do very effectively, which is understanding visual information,” says Kim.

Rather than choosing one or the other, some firms are using a mix of open-weight and closed-weight AI models.

Eu Leong Oh, medical director at The Longevity Suite Asia, a Singapore-based wellness clinic, states he’s using Claude and Google’s Gemini to build the team’s in-house healthcare portal, but plans to pivot to open-weight models for daily use. “For things like prototyping, exploration and research, it’s still very useful to have a large-parameter, trained, closed-weight model,” Oh says.

Recent findings suggest that he compares a top-tier frontier model to a Michelin-starred chef. “You’ll want a chef like Gordon Ramsay to decide the processes in your restaurant, but you don’t need him to do the cooking all the time,” he indicates. “Similarly, within companies, a lot of the heavy lifting and token budget will eventually be taken over by more cost effective open-weight models.”.

Token costs are also skyrocketing with the rise of agentic AI. An AI agent might consume five times more tokens than a chatbot interface, because it runs multi-step loops rather than a single task. Those increasing costs may push companies to adopt cheaper open-weight models on top of existing closed-weight ones.

It has been revealed that “Companies are becoming more cost-conscious about their AI deployment,” claims Srividya Jandhyala, a professor of management at ESSEC Business School. “Not every task needs the power of a frontier model, and companies are recognizing that ‘good enough’ models work for a large variety of operations.”.

In a recent development, yet a tech giant’s decision whether or not to use an open-weight model could come down to politics, rather than cost or technical ability. The leading open-weight models come from Chinese companies like DeepSeek, Alibaba, and z.AI; their growing usage in both U.S. and global business is worrying some in Washington about China’s growing influence over the technology.

Sources indicate that “The American AI stack remains far stronger than China’s and we must continue to lead,” Representative John Moolenaar (R-Mich.), chair of the U.S. House’s Select Committee on China, wrote in a Sept. 23 statement.

According to recent reports, on Nov. 18, Reuters reported that the Trump administration was considering requiring U.S. firms to publicly disclose their use of Chinese AI models, in hopes of discouraging use of the technology without imposing upcoming restrictions that might anger Beijing.

Industry observers note that in a Nov. 20 report, Moolenaar warned that American businesses were adopting inexpensive Chinese AI models. “Federal investigations, however, have found that major PRC developers used proxy networks and fraudulent accounts to harvest outputs from American frontier models and replicate their capabilities. While America is investing billions and racing to build ‘Super Intelligence,’ Beijing is using stolen intelligence to close the gap,” he wrote.

Cursor—whose Composer coding agent was built on Moonshot’s Kimi model—told Congress that it’s considering phasing out Chinese AI models due to “geopolitical risk,” CNBC reported.

Industry observers note that “For global companies, especially in Western markets, there is a trade-off between cheaper Chinese alternatives versus concerns about continued access,” explains Jandhyala of ESSEC. “If they think that future policies may force them to reduce their reliance on Chinese AI models, companies may pre-emptively start using U.S. open- or closed-weight models.”.

In a recent development, A handful of U.S. companies—including Thinking Machines, Reflection AI and Nvidia—are releasing open-weight models. Nvidia and its recently returned CEO, Jensen Huang, have also championed the technology. According to Reuters, Huang’s support for open-weight AI helped persuade Trump and Vice President JD Vance to push for his return.

The concern that Chinese models may come with hidden backdoors may be overstated, claims Erik Cambria, a professor of AI at Singapore’s Nanyang Technological University (NTU).

“Concerns about Chinese models should be distinguished between genuine technical security risks and geopolitical perceptions,” he claims. “An open-weight model deployed locally, without transmitting sensitive data externally, presents a very different risk profile from a remotely hosted API, regardless of the model’s country of origin.”.

In a recent development, still, geopolitical concerns may drive companies to diversify where they get their models from. “Europeans optimize for sovereignty and compliance,” says Groth of UC Berkeley. “In Asia and the Gulf, pragmatists hedge across both stacks and refuse to pick a side, unless they need models and applications which implicate national security.”.

For businesses, the goal may not be picking a winner in the AI race, but keeping their options open. “Businesses will combine models from different providers and select the most appropriate one for each workload,” says Cambria.

What’s Next For Recruiting, Job Hunting And HR? More AI, Of Course

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (803 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crunchbase

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that AI agents and humanoid robots may dominate the funding headlines.
  • In a recent development, so far this year, venture backers have poured close to $4 billion into an assortment of global companies focused on recruiting, finding jobs and streamlining processes associated with HR and payroll management, Crunchbase data demonstrates.
  • To get a sense where capital is flowing, we used Crunchbase data to analyze investment to employment-related categories for the past few years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that AI agents and humanoid robots may dominate the funding headlines. But even so, investors haven’t lost interest in startups focused on finding, filling and managing jobs for actual humans.

In a recent development, so far this year, venture backers have poured close to $4 billion into an assortment of global companies focused on recruiting, finding jobs and streamlining processes associated with HR and payroll management, Crunchbase data demonstrates. Not surprisingly, the vast majority are also incorporating a heavy dose of AI.

To get a sense where capital is flowing, we used Crunchbase data to analyze investment to employment-related categories for the past few years. Broadly, findings show 2026 funding on track to meet or slightly exceed year-ago levels, albeit with reduced deal count.

Recent findings suggest that much of this year’s investment has gone to a small group of companies. To illustrate, below we put together a list of 14 of the largest fundraisers.

As you can see, it’s a varied list, with a commonly shared theme of bringing more automation to hiring, HR and payroll tasks.

Industry observers note that by far the largest funding recipient is Mercor, a startup that pairs human experts with developers of AI models and tools. The 4-year-old company raised $750 million in a Series D round this month at a whopping $20 billion valuation.

According to recent reports, san Francisco-based Mercor is betting that as companies build AI agents to take on more work tasks, demand for subject matter experts to guide these efforts will grow. While frontier labs have been its primary buyers for the past few years, Mercor states it expects enterprises will soon be its major customers.

It has been revealed that the next two largest fundraisers on our list for this year are focused on automating more employer tasks. Paris-based Skello secured $220 million this summer for its AI-enabled software platform for HR teams. And HiBob, a New York-based platform for HR and payroll, picked up $166 million in a Salesforce1-led financing.

Industry observers note that of course, investors aren’t only looking at startups automating work tasks or training AI agents to do so. They’re also backing companies focused on the old-fashioned business of matching workers and employers.

In this sector, one of the larger rounds this year went to San Francisco-based Juicebox, an AI tool for recruiters to find talented candidates. The 4-year-old company picked up an $80 million Series B at an $850 million valuation.

In a recent development, agentic hiring is also a thing. Metaview, a San Francisco-based startup that offers an agentic recruiting platform optimized, in its words, to “get the right butts in seats,” secured $60 million in a September Series C financing. Around the same time, London’s Jack & Jill AI, which offers AI agents for finding careers and for hiring, closed on $40 million in Series A funding.

Another agentic hiring platform, San Francisco’s Paraform, announced a $40 million round this spring, pitching itself as an offering for an age in which employers are making fewer hires overall but still need highly skilled people for highly paid jobs.

So what kind of employment future do startup funding trends paint for human jobseekers?

Industry observers note that not a good one. As a human who has spent decades writing about sector-specific startup funding, this is probably the most depressing data dive into investment trends for an industry that I have ever done.

Overall, the bulk of big rounds are going to one of three categories: using humans to help train their potential AI replacements, automating work tasks around supporting people in the workplace, and getting AI to help hire the right people for the dwindling pool of available positions.

Typically, I’m rooting for startups to succeed. And honestly, there’s not an individual tech giant highlighted here that I’m specifically hoping will fail. But nonetheless, the broad vision of an increasingly AI-dominated workplace does bring with it a sense of trepidation.

According to recent reports, thankfully, XRP shows us resilience beyond regular market metrics: the average daily payments throughout the month have crossed the 1.1 million threshold, a 107% growth versus the October baseline. The basis behind the reversal is considerable: the rise in market volatility that triggered a substantial breakdown in the asset.

In a recent development, with rapid market swings, it's no surprise that the asset saw more than 1.33 million transactions throughout the first 7 days of the month. Latest accounts over a rolling 24-hour period reached 4,065 wallets, per XRPScan query on November 23.

Sources indicate that from the technical standpoint, XRP is currently trading near the $0.99 price level, approximately 23% lower compared to the 30-day average, which fits the aforementioned bearish narrative. The decline in spot trading volume is also an crucial sign: spot investors dropped around 22.5% of their trading activities throughout the month.

Recent findings suggest that the drop in futures volume also makes the picture slightly more complicated than it should be. Following the price breakdown, the volatility increase was followed by an increase in open interest, so the drop we're witnessing right now is more of a return to the baseline than an concern on its own.

The current price resistance and support points are quite diverse, but not thoroughly tested, apart from a local support level at $0.9. The immediate breakout test is going to take place at approximately $0.99, with a possibility of a further recovery. Recent findings suggest that are Ripple’s XRP, Cardano (ADA), and Polygon (POL) losing their appeal among crypto investors in 2026? In his post on X, Simpson acknowledged XRP’s role in enabling near-instant, inexpensive payments on the XRP Ledger but argued that the token lacks a compelling mechanism for capturing the value generated by Ripple’s business growth.

Recent findings suggest that he also pointed out that Ripple does not use its business earnings to buy back XRP, a mechanism that could potentially create additional demand for the token. For Simpson, the absence of both profit-sharing and a buyback program makes it difficult to establish a direct link between Ripple’s growing business and XRP’s price in the long term.

He considers these shortcomings significant enough to keep XRP off his investment list, despite the network’s payment capabilities.

Sources indicate that simpson also expressed reservations about Cardano, arguing that its adoption level does not justify its market valuation. Although ADA powers a blockchain designed to support smart contracts and decentralized applications, he believes the network is generating relatively little economic activity compared with its overall market size.

To support his argument, Simpson pointed to Cardano’s fee generation, claiming that the network collected just $140,000 in transaction fees over a 30-day period despite ADA carrying a market capitalization of approximately $7.5 billion.

For him, the disparity raises questions about whether Cardano is attracting enough people and developers to sustain its valuation. He believes a blockchain with such a substantial market capitalization should demonstrate considerably stronger usage and demand for its services.

Sources indicate that ultimately, Simpson’s concern is that Cardano needs to translate its technological ambitions and established ecosystem into greater real-world activity. Without a meaningful increase in network usage, he appears unconvinced that ADA offers an attractive investment proposition.

Polygon also made the list, with concerns centered on the growing competition in Ethereum’s scaling ecosystem. Although POL supports a network designed to make transactions faster and cheaper, the increasing number of competing blockchain solutions has made it harder for Polygon to maintain a distinctive advantage.

Simpson’s concern is that newer networks are offering similar benefits, including lower transaction costs and faster processing speeds, leaving Polygon with fewer obvious ways to differentiate itself.

With several projects competing for developers, owners, and blockchain activity, POL faces the challenge of proving why it deserves a place ahead of its rivals.

He argued that strong sector potential means little without meaningful retail participation.

His experience with WIF appears to have reinforced his preference for cryptocurrencies backed by stronger fundamentals rather than speculative excitement.

Breaking: webAI Releases TwIL-8B: A 5 GiB Open-Weight Reasoning Model With a 98.2 MATH-500 Score

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1127 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • webAI's open-weight TwIL-8B posts 98.2 on MATH-500 and says it tops Gemma 4 31B.
  • A model small enough to run from a roughly 5 GiB file on a CPU now claims a 98.2 on MATH-500.
  • Industry observers note that webAI released TwIL-8B as an open-weight model on November 4, and its Hugging Face model card leads with ambitious numbers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

webAI's open-weight TwIL-8B posts 98.2 on MATH-500 and says it tops Gemma 4 31B. The card's own footnotes show why the comparison deserves a re-run.

A model small enough to run from a roughly 5 GiB file on a CPU now claims a 98.2 on MATH-500. The most revealing line in its model card isn't a score, though. It's a footnote saying the competitor numbers were never re-run.

Industry observers note that webAI released TwIL-8B as an open-weight model on November 4, and its Hugging Face model card leads with ambitious numbers. The 8.8B-parameter reasoning model is post-trained from IBM's Granite 4.2 8B using full-parameter supervised fine-tuning, followed by GRPO/DAPO reinforcement learning. A final length-aware RL stage produces the "balanced" variant, which is the default.

The card reports 98.2 on MATH-500 and 88.3 on AIME 2025. It notes TwIL-8B posts the highest MATH-500 and LiveCodeBench scores in its comparison group, which includes Gemma 4 31B at about 3.5 times its size. That claim is worth testing, because small models that beat larger ones are exactly what open-weight owners want to hear.

Sources indicate that on MATH-500, the card lists TwIL-8B at 98.2, Qwen3.5-9B at 96.6 and Gemma 4 31B at 87.9. On AIME 2025, TwIL-8B scores 88.3 against 87.1 for Gemma 4 31B. On LiveCodeBench, TwIL-8B scores 81.6 against 80.0, though that figure carries a dagger marking it as measured on the verbose variant, not the default balanced one.

According to recent reports, the card is also more candid than most. It notes TwIL-8B is not a knowledge model. GPQA Diamond comes in at 70.2, trailing Gemma 4 31B by 14.1 points, and the model also trails on MMLU-Pro and HLE. There is no safety or preference tuning beyond what Granite carries, and the license is non-commercial. That honesty makes the claims easier to weigh.

Recent findings suggest that here is where the headline gets complicated. TwIL-8B's scores come from webAI's own internal high-effort pass@1 runs. The card states that competitor scores are published figures and were not re-run.

According to recent reports, gemma 4 31B's 87.9 on MATH-500 comes from Red Hat's evaluation of an FP8 build, using the lighteval harness, not from Google. The card itself notes that this figure is unusually low and may reflect answer extraction. In other words, the 10.3-point gap that anchors the headline compares one team's own harness against a third party's number that the card suspects may be understated.

It has been revealed that none of this makes TwIL-8B's result wrong. It means the margin isn't established until both models run under the same harness, prompt and sampling settings. For reference, Google's Gemma 4 model card is the source for several of the other Gemma figures in the table.

Read the whole table and the picture is more balanced than the headline suggests. In the card's head-to-head summary, TwIL-8B beats Gemma 4 31B on 3 of 14 shared benchmarks and loses 11. It leads on MATH-500, LiveCodeBench and AIME 2025, but trails on AIME 2026 (88.3 against 89.2), HMMT Feb 2026 (68.2 against 77.2), GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro and IFEval.

The AIME 2025 lead is the shakiest. The card claims AIME and HMMT sets have 30 to 33 problems, so one problem is worth about 3 points, and gaps of that size sit within noise. A 1.2-point margin is well under one problem, so the result is best read as a tie.

Against the closest same-size rival, Qwen3.5-9B, the card demonstrates the models roughly level on contest math, with TwIL-8B using fewer tokens: about 19.5k per AIME 2026 problem against 31.2k. That efficiency claim may turn out to be the more durable one.

The card makes replication unusually practical. The Q4_K_M balanced GGUF weighs 4.98 GiB and runs through llama.cpp, with a command given in the card. Larger Q8_0 and F16 builds exist only for the verbose variant. The model also needs a major generation budget, since a short limit truncates its reasoning and scores far worse. The card suggests settings around 32,768 upcoming tokens and a 40,960-token context.

Anyone planning a check should expect three catches. First, the card states all its scores were measured on bf16 weights, not the GGUF builds, so a CPU run tests a slightly different artifact, and the card expects small deviations, most likely at Q4_K_M. Second, MATH-500 is 500 problems and each answer can run to tens of thousands of tokens, so CPU testing will be slow. Third, the decoding setup matters, since the card says none of its numbers use low-effort or thinking-off modes.

For a fair comparison, the same prompt, answer extraction and sampling must be applied to Gemma 4 31B too, ideally at full precision.

The card also lists contamination caveats. Its training pools were decontaminated against AIME, HMMT Feb 2025 and 2026, MATH-500, GPQA, MMLU-Pro, HLE, IFEval, IFBench and LiveCodeBench using 13-gram matching. HMMT Nov 2025 and the HumanEval, MBPP and CRUXEval suites weren't in the decontamination set. The MATH-500 and AIME results fall inside the protected group, which counts in the model's favor.

Overall, TwIL-8B looks like a genuinely strong small model for contest math, code and instruction following, and the card is open about its weak spots. The claim to beat Gemma 4 31B is narrower than the headline suggests: a clear lead on one benchmark, a likely tie on another and a loss on most of the rest.

The useful next step is a same-harness run of both models, with the bf16 weights as a control for the GGUF build. Until independent results appear, the 98.2 is best quoted as webAI's reported figure, and the size-beating framing is better described as unproven than wrong.

Should You Run Your Own AI or Pay a Provider? Here’s How to Decide.

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1154 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • I’m an AI engineer and I’m right now building ChatMakr, an AI-powered platform that creates multi-agent chatbots in seconds, powered by open-weight models.
  • An open-weight model is a model whose trained parameters are published for anyone to download and run, without necessarily sharing the code or data used to train it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

I’m an AI engineer and I’m right now building ChatMakr, an AI-powered platform that creates multi-agent chatbots in seconds, powered by open-weight models. I also spent time at a consulting firm focused on innovation financing, where I talked with hundreds of Parisian entrepreneurs, and this exact question — run it yourself or rent it from someone else — came up constantly. Open-weight models have made that question sharper than ever, so here’s how to actually think through it.

An open-weight model is a model whose trained parameters are published for anyone to download and run, without necessarily sharing the code or data used to train it. As the Open Source Initiative defines it, “Open Weights refer to the final weights and biases of a trained neural network.” You get the finished brain, not the recipe that built it. That distinction is exactly why open-weight models matter for this decision: because you can download the weights, you’re free to run them on your own hardware, on a cloud provider’s hardware or switch between the two, instead of being locked into one company’s API.

In a recent development, self-hosting means running that open-weight model on infrastructure you control, whether that’s a GPU server sitting in your own office or a rented GPU virtual machine you fully manage. You pick the hardware, you install the software and you’re responsible for keeping it running.

According to recent reports, cloud means renting inference from a provider instead, whether that’s a managed endpoint hosting an open-weight model for you or a closed API you call over the internet. But cloud isn’t one single choice, because where that provider is headquartered changes what legal system governs your data. A U.S. cloud provider, even one running a data center inside the EU, remains bound by the CLOUD Act.

In a recent development, here’s how it actually plays out. Below, I’ll call the winner between self-host and cloud on six specific fronts.

Industry observers note that self-hosting looks expensive on paper because you’re paying for a GPU whether you use it or not, but at high enough volume that fixed cost stops mattering. Cloudzy’s cost analysis explains that “self-hosting an open-weight model on a GPU VPS can beat a frontier API at high, sustained volume with good GPU utilization.” The catch is that most businesses never generate that kind of steady, maxed-out traffic. For anyone below that threshold, cloud wins on cost.

Recent findings suggest that running your own GPUs doesn’t just cost hardware money, it costs people, and that line item is easy to underestimate. Activepieces breaks down the real total cost of ownership and finds that “the payroll for these positions often exceeds the annual budget for the H100 GPUs they manage.” The engineers who keep a self-hosted stack alive frequently cost more than the chips they’re maintaining. Cloud wins here, because the provider absorbs that staffing burden for you.

For businesses handling sensitive or regulated data, who can legally compel access to your information matters as much as who can technically breach it. MassiveGRID lays out the jurisdiction problem plainly: “a U.S.-headquartered provider operating servers in the EU is still subject to the CLOUD Act,” while “a provider incorporated and operating entirely within the EU provides stronger protection against extraterritorial data access requests.” Self-hosting on your own hardware or choosing an EU-only cloud provider closes off that exposure entirely. Self-hosting, or EU cloud specifically, wins on legal exposure.

Industry observers note that demand for AI products rarely arrives in a straight line, and that’s where renting infrastructure pays off. Buzzclan defines the core benefit of cloud elasticity as “the ability to automatically adjust infrastructure capacity based on demand, helping businesses maintain performance without overprovisioning.” A self-hosted GPU server can’t grow on demand during a traffic spike or shrink back down when things go quiet, it just sits at whatever size you bought it at. Cloud wins on scalability.

Open-weight models exist precisely because businesses want to shape the model itself, not just prompt around its limits. A closed cloud API gives you a fixed model behind a fixed interface. Self-hosting wins on customization.

For a business selling into enterprise customers, a provider’s paperwork can matter as much as its performance. Google Cloud explains what its SOC 2 report actually verifies: “the SOC 2 reports are generated by an objective third party attesting to a set of assertions made by Google Cloud about its controls that are in place to protect customer data.” Building that same audited trail yourself, on your own servers, takes real time and specialized staff most startups don’t have. Cloud wins on compliance.

It has been revealed that there’s no single winner here, and that’s the actual takeaway. Open-weight models made this a genuine choice instead of a forced one: The same model can run in a rented data center or on a box you own, and the right answer depends on which of these six factors matters most to your business right now.

It has been revealed that if you’re regulated or handling sensitive data, lean self-host or EU cloud. If you’re scaling unpredictably or don’t want to hire an infrastructure team, lean cloud. Most businesses will end up doing both — cloud for the unpredictable parts, self-hosting for the parts that need full control — and that’s not indecision; it’s just matching the infrastructure to the actual argument that matters most in each case.

Industry News: Can Institutions Secretly Buy Billions of XRP? Ripple Veteran Says It Is 'Not Impossible'

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (408 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: U

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ripple’s longtime CTO emeritus David Schwartz does not think institutions can privately snap up billions of XRP via dark pools without affecting the token’s price on public markets.
  • Why wouldn't people generally want the price to rise when they buy?
  • This was in response to a question posed by an XRP community member wondering if private trading platforms might give institutions an advantage over retail investors.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ripple’s longtime CTO emeritus David Schwartz does not think institutions can privately snap up billions of XRP via dark pools without affecting the token’s price on public markets.

"I don't think so. Who are they buying the XRP from? Why wouldn't people generally want the price to rise when they buy? But it's not impossible," Schwartz wrote on X on Nov. 24.

This was in response to a question posed by an XRP community member wondering if private trading platforms might give institutions an advantage over retail investors.

Earlier in the conversation, Schwartz noted the pros and cons of dark pools for retail traders.

He mentioned one disadvantage: less efficient price discovery. Given that bids and offers are obscured, retail traders in public markets have less insight into other traders’ bids and ask prices.

According to recent reports, if there is a large XRP holder who is already inclined to sell at the current price, an institution could arrange a private trade with this holder without needing to place a massive buy order on an exchange. They could execute the trade without driving the public price up as they buy.

According to recent reports, however, will there be enough sellers interested in offloading billions of XRP like this? One might run out of sellers willing to sell at that price. So, the buyer might need to up the ante to find the next willing seller.

A dark pool can hide order size, but one still needs someone on the other side to execute that order.

Plus, a buyer will naturally prefer not to tip its hand while accumulating a position.

Schwartz left open the possibility of a private purchase at scale, but the possibility is rather low.

When asked why XRP Ledger developments were not doing anything for XRP’s price on Nov. 9, Schwartz pointed to the broader crypto market.

Recent findings suggest that he also debunked the notion that Ripple had some secret plan it was not sharing with holders. The tech giant regularly talks about its plans.

Schwartz also mentioned a practical benefit of XRP being worth more in the: a higher price could mean cheaper liquidity provision and less slippage (the difference between the expected price a trader pays and the price they actually pay).

At the same time, he was less convinced that demand for XRP to pay transaction fees could have a substantial impact on the price by itself.

Breaking: Amazon is buying Decart’s AI chip software for a reported $7.5B and bringing its founders aboard

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (681 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 8:25 amNovember 23, 2026 at 8:27 am.
  • Amazon confirmed Monday morning that it will acquire Decart’s AI optimization technology, known as the Decart Optimization Stack, and bring on the 3-year-old startup’s founders and team of AI researchers and engineers.
  • According to recent reports, amazon didn’t disclose financial terms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 8:25 amNovember 23, 2026 at 8:27 am.

Amazon confirmed Monday morning that it will acquire Decart’s AI optimization technology, known as the Decart Optimization Stack, and bring on the 3-year-old startup’s founders and team of AI researchers and engineers.

According to recent reports, amazon didn’t disclose financial terms. Amazon agreed to pay about $7.5 billion for the assets, Bloomberg reported, citing a person familiar with the matter. The deal is tied to performance targets over five years, Globes reported.

It has been revealed that the deal could boost Amazon’s push to compete with Nvidia, which sells most of the chips used for training and running AI models today. Amazon makes its own AI chips, called Trainium, and has signaled prepares to start selling them directly to other companies, beyond its own AWS data centers.

“We believe we’re going to have a very significant business selling chips externally,” CEO Andy Jassy mentioned on the company’s earnings call last month.

Amazon announced the deal the same day Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, ending a leadership shakeup at the chipmaker that put CFO Colette Kress in the interim role.

Sources indicate that decart’s software is designed to get more performance out of each chip, one of the main selling points Amazon needs to win those external customers. Microsoft is building its own Maia chips, mainly for its own AI services, and Google has its TPUs.

In a recent development, decart’s software has also run on chips from Nvidia and Google. Amazon didn’t say whether that will continue.

“Every leap forward in AI starts with getting more out of every chip,” said Peter DeSantis, Amazon’s senior vice president of foundational AI models, custom silicon and quantum computing, in the blog post announcing the acquisition.

Decart’s three co-founders are joining Amazon: CEO Dean Leitersdorf, his brother Orian Leitersdorf and Moshe Shalev. Amazon isn’t buying Decart’s AI models, Bloomberg reported. Those include Lucy, which edits live video in real time, and Oasis, which generates interactive virtual worlds.

Recent findings suggest that the deal runs through Annapurna Labs, Amazon’s chip unit, and Decart’s technology will be used to improve performance on Amazon’s Trainium and Inferentia AI chips, according to Globes. The Israeli business publication reported that Annapurna co-founder Nafea Bshara led the negotiations for Amazon.

The founders, who own about 64% of Decart, have committed to stay at Amazon for five years and could receive about $4.8 billion collectively, Globes reported.

In a recent development, amazon bought Annapurna, also founded in Israel, in 2015 for a reported $350 million. Its engineers went on to design Trainium and Amazon’s other custom chips.

In a recent development, amazon and Decart have worked together since 2025. Decart was among the first customers on Trainium3, and Amazon said last December that Decart was running real-time video four times faster on Trainium at half the cost of GPUs.

The deal follows Amazon’s release last month of TorchNeuron, a tool that runs common AI code on Trainium with minimal changes. Both moves target the software advantage that has kept developers on Nvidia hardware, as GeekWire explained when the talks surfaced in October.

It has been revealed that decart drew interest from other massive buyers before Amazon. Anthropic was in talks to acquire it for about $6 billion, Bloomberg reported in August, before it walked away in September. Nvidia held earlier acquisition talks, according to CTech, and invested in Decart’s $300 million funding round in May.

In a recent development, “From day one, our mission has been to redefine the boundaries of what AI can do and to make it dramatically more efficient along the way,” Dean Leitersdorf mentioned in Amazon’s announcement. “Joining Amazon gives our team the scale, the customers, and the infrastructure to pursue that mission faster than we could on our own.”.

According to recent reports, the deal is subject to regulatory clearance. Amazon didn’t say what happens to Decart’s AI models or to its existing customers, such as eBay, which is also an investor in the startup.

  • For startups, that means opportunities to modernize how we move goods, produce energy and manage marine resources.
  • Sources indicate that the blue economy has doubled in size in just a quarter of a century, reaching $2.6 trillion in value.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The “blue economy,” which encompasses industries built around oceans and coasts — from shipping and fisheries to offshore energy and marine biotechnology — is one of the largest, yet least visible, engines of the global economy.

For startups, that means opportunities to modernize how we move goods, produce energy and manage marine resources.

Sources indicate that the blue economy has doubled in size in just a quarter of a century, reaching $2.6 trillion in value. To put this in perspective: If the blue economy were a country, it would be the world’s fifth largest. And as the world turns back to the sea to face increasingly critical challenges, from geopolitical instability to rising energy prices and climate resilience, the blue economy is set to become even more central.

In a recent development, powerful “blue technology” forces of disruption are at play. Digitalization and automation, the energy transition, environmental pressures and advances in marine biotechnology are all reshaping how value is created at sea.

Investment in those technologies is also accelerating, with an emphasis on sustainable development. Blue tech companies tracked in Mind the Bridge’s “Rethinking the Blue Economy” report, produced with support from Crunchbase, raised almost $10 billion through the third quarter of 2026 — already exceeding the $6.2 billion raised in all of 2025. Large rounds for defense companies with maritime applications account for much of that surge.

According to recent reports, against the prevailing trend in the global innovation landscape, blue tech has followed a substantially continuous upward trajectory since 2021, producing an average of 70 new scaleups per year — even more rapidly over the past two years. Preliminary figures for 2026 suggest that roughly 100 new blue tech scaleups may emerge by year-end.

The same trend is evident in funding figures. In 2025, blue tech funding has reached $6.2 billion, double than the previous year. As of Q3 2026, blue tech scaleups worldwide had already raised almost $10 billion in latest capital. If this trend continues, we expect the sector to attract more than $12 billion by year-end.

Sources indicate that the drivers? Exceptional maritime resilience deals involving defense and infrastructure companies such as Anduril Industries ($5 billion raised in 2026) and Helsing ($1.8 billion raised in 2026).

Sources indicate that blue tech is a broad category including a diverse set of technologies, some of which are more mature than others. To shed light on the sector’s composition, we clustered each unique technology developed by blue tech scaleups into 20 groups.

We then assessed each group from two different perspectives: impact on the industry and market commitment (a combination of scaleup and capital invested density).

The result is a matrix highlighting:.

The other quadrants are populated by transversal technologies with a more indirect impact on the industry and emerging niche technologies.

The ultimate question is: Who will ride the wave of change of the Blue Economy?

Ports are where the dynamics reshaping maritime activities converge most visibly, acting as mini “blue economies.” In many ways, ports are the “smartest smart cities” — dense, complex systems where energy, logistics, data, mobility and people meet. They are places where innovation can be tested at scale before spreading to the wider economy.

And like smart cities a decade ago, they now need a playbook.

To provide a comprehensive perspective from the ports’ point of view, in our report we interviewed 10 of the world’s leading port authorities to understand their priorities, challenges and barriers to innovation.

While doing so, we collected several case studies from authorities such as the ports of Barcelona, Bergen, Seattle, Rotterdam and Los Angeles — true blueprints of best practices in tackling the innovation challenges of the blue economy.

The result is a picture that demonstrates the potential of blue tech as the catalyst for a radical evolution of one of the largest sectors of the global economy.

To “ride the wave,” most ports are already activating multiple open innovation tools — some with a structured approach and dedicated units.

Yet, to really “get there” port authorities, operators, startups, investors and policymakers need a shared agenda and vision, working on the same challenges.

Early but substantial efforts are already underway. A prime example is BlueTechPort by the Port of Barcelona, a collaborative innovation hub connecting entrepreneurs, technology providers, researchers and maritime businesses. The initiative, detailed in a full case study available in the report, is already expanding internationally through the Lighthouse International Acceleration Program, powered by Mind the Bridge.

Industry observers note that notice to (innovation) sailors: the course of blue economy innovation is set. The challenge now is to catch the favorable winds — and ride them.

The Simple AI Framework I Use to Cut Administrative Waste

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • When I opened my first physical therapy practice, I believed growth depended on seeing more patients.
  • Years later, after building therapy, staffing and hospice companies, I see artificial intelligence the same way I see any business tool: Its value comes from solving a real operational problem.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

When I opened my first physical therapy practice, I believed growth depended on seeing more patients. That mindset worked for a while, until I realized my team and I were spending hours every day on paperwork, scheduling and insurance tasks instead of patient care. Administrative work had quietly become the biggest obstacle to growth.

Years later, after building therapy, staffing and hospice companies, I see artificial intelligence the same way I see any business tool: Its value comes from solving a real operational problem. AI should give your people more time to serve customers and build relationships. Everything else is secondary. That philosophy has shaped how we use technology across our businesses.

Sources indicate that spend a week identifying every repetitive task that eats up valuable time. Look for work that follows the same steps every day and requires little judgment. Those processes usually deliver the fastest return when automated.

In health care, charting, appointment scheduling and insurance verification rapidly rose to the top of our list. Every industry has its own version of these tasks. Find them before you buy any technology.

Resist the urge to automate everything at once. Doing so can overwhelm you and your team, and it makes it hard to tell which changes worked and which flopped.

In a recent development, start with the one to three administrative processes that consume the most hours each week. For us, documentation was the obvious first choice. AI-assisted transcription dramatically reduced the time clinicians spent writing notes, so they could focus on patients instead of keyboards.

Sources indicate that we also introduced AI tools for scheduling and insurance verification. Those systems reduced delays and freed employees to handle conversations that required empathy and critical thinking.

In a recent development, many leaders evaluate AI by asking whether the software costs less than another employee. I prefer a different question: How many productive hours did the technology return to the business?

Recent findings suggest that if documentation falls from 30 minutes to five minutes per appointment, those recovered hours create measurable capacity. Teams can serve more customers, improve quality or simply leave work on time. Revenue often follows, but the first win is reclaimed time.

Tracking time savings also keeps expectations realistic. Every automation project should produce measurable improvements before you expand it to another department.

Every AI project deserves a simple scorecard. Track how many hours employees save each week, how swiftly customers get a response, how many errors disappear from the process and how your team feels after the change. Those measurements show whether the technology is delivering real value or just adding another subscription to the budget.

Review these metrics every month. Small improvements often compound into significant operational gains over time. Consistent measurement also helps employees see the purpose behind each fresh tool, which builds confidence and speeds adoption across the organization.

It has been revealed that burnout rarely begins with meaningful work. It usually begins with repetitive work.

It has been revealed that few health care professionals entered the field because they loved paperwork, and entrepreneurs in every industry can relate. Endless administrative duties drain energy that could go to customers, employees or strategic planning.

When AI removes repetitive work, people get back to the work that inspired them in the first place, and burnout drops as a result. In our businesses, clinicians give more attention to patient conversations because documentation happens in the background. That shift improves both the employee experience and the customer experience.

Successful adoption comes from discipline, not speed. Begin with one department. Select one workflow. Define one success metric. Once that process delivers consistent results, move on to the next opportunity.

This phased approach builds confidence throughout the organization. Employees see practical improvements instead of another technology initiative that creates extra work. Leaders also gain reliable data before making larger investments.

Small wins create momentum that large transformations rarely achieve on day one.

Industry observers note that one common misconception is that AI is meant to replace people. It isn’t.

Industry observers note that technology should strengthen human capability, not replace human judgment. Every automation decision we make comes back to the same question: Will this give our people more time for work that requires experience, compassion and creative thinking?

It has been revealed that that principle has guided our investments, from AI documentation to administrative automation. Technology handles repetition. People handle relationships. Together, they build stronger businesses than either could alone.

Sources indicate that once we put these changes in place, the difference was almost immediate. Clinicians spent less time on documentation after appointments and more time engaging with patients during them. Front office teams fielded fewer routine calls because scheduling and administrative questions moved through AI-powered workflows, which reduced delays and made the experience smoother for everyone.

According to recent reports, what surprised me most was the ripple effect. Employees felt less overwhelmed because they could focus on work that required their expertise. Leaders had better visibility into operations because we were measuring performance instead of reacting to problems. Those improvements gave us the confidence to expand AI into other areas of the business, one process at a time.

Industry observers note that the experience reinforced something I’ve believed throughout my career: Sustainable growth comes from building systems that free talented people to do what they do best. AI became one more tool that helped us deliver better care, strengthen our operations and prepare our businesses for the next stage of growth.

Latest Update: Island is a upcoming screen-time app that turns staying off your phone into a game

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A new startup is taking a different approach to helping people manage their screen time.
  • This carrot-instead-of-stick approach was dreamed up by entrepreneurs Ashish Selvaraj (CEO) and Ethan Pronev (CTO), who met while studying at the University of Waterloo, then went on to work at companies that included Jane Street, Citadel Securities, Databricks, and Microsoft.
  • Later, they quit their jobs to join the startup accelerator Y Combinator, where they first tried out other ideas in areas like B2B and software-as-a-service, but weren’t finding the right fit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A new startup is taking a different approach to helping people manage their screen time. Instead of blocking apps or restricting the phone’s use after a set period, an app called Island encourages you to meet your screen time goals by way of a farming simulator game. Yes, a game! Island works by rewarding you when you’re disciplined enough to meet your goals with a “credit score” that increases your farm’s production, unlocking new crops, animals, and other content.

This carrot-instead-of-stick approach was dreamed up by entrepreneurs Ashish Selvaraj (CEO) and Ethan Pronev (CTO), who met while studying at the University of Waterloo, then went on to work at companies that included Jane Street, Citadel Securities, Databricks, and Microsoft.

Later, they quit their jobs to join the startup accelerator Y Combinator, where they first tried out other ideas in areas like B2B and software-as-a-service, but weren’t finding the right fit.

Island ended up being their fifth pivot, and the first the founders actually found themselves enjoying.

“Once we were in YC, I think there’s a big mindset — I think in [San Francisco], in general — of, ‘selling shovels.’ Everyone wants to ‘sell shovels’ to other companies, and around us, that’s just what was going on,” explains Selvaraj, speaking about the concept that many successful startups sell the tools, infrastructure, or services to others following whatever the current market boom or trend may be.

“So all the ideas we had — we tried these things — but we found that we weren’t passionate about it. Like idea after idea seemed like ultimately the product was just a dashboard with some kind of different backend,” he added. “It felt like we quit our jobs … just to do something that was a variation of that.”.

With Island, the team gets to tap into their creativity, having drawn the pixel art themselves.

“A lot of people do use [AI] models to generate the art, but we felt that it had a certain character when we drew it ourselves,” he told TechCrunch. “I feel like with Claude getting so good, there’s a tendency to give away every task to Claude. But ultimately it feels like there’s something else that comes out when you do it yourself, especially in something like art,” Selvaraj said.

According to recent reports, what’s more, the app does appear to be successful in helping people meet their goals, the startup’s early data highlights. After early testing and an October launch, the team notes that the majority of its users (82%) will end their screen time right at the limit they’ve set. Many more are ending their screen time when they get the “15 minutes left” warning.

According to recent reports, island could appeal to those who have given up on other screen time apps out of frustration because the app doesn’t actually lock you out of apps or your phone. That’s something that can end up being more disruptive, especially when you’re in the middle of doing something, like posting, sharing, commenting, or chatting, among other things. Instead, Island taps into people’ own self-discipline and their desire to see their island flourish to encourage screen time breaks.

The idea to encourage customers to keep their goals by offering some other type of in-app reward system isn’t entirely novel. Last year, Hank Green’s screen time app Focus Friend went viral for its experience, which involved a little friend that could only knit items that, in turn, allowed you to get points used to decorate your room when you were focused on your non-distracting apps.

Industry observers note that similar ideas have been used in self-care apps and habit-trackers like Finch, Amaru, Belly, Flora, Urso, and others. But Island expands this concept from being focused on helping out a virtual friend or pet to one that’s more of a game — and one where you can experience the consequences without “having to torture your pet,” notes Selvaraj.

Island also allows owners to add friends and visit each other’s islands, compete in group challenges, and keep each other accountable by tying your island together with one friend of your choosing. In the latter scenario, if either friend goes over their limit, both of their islands will suffer.

The startup indicates Island has proven to be fairly “sticky” with a 51% daily active owners-to-monthly active users ratio, and a day 30 retention rate of 49%, meaning 49% of users were still active on the app on the 30th day since the app was installed.

In a recent development, the app is currently free to use, with a $39.99 per year subscription that allows you to set individual limits on different apps, instead of just an overall daily screen time limit. The organization hasn’t raised additional seed funding outside of YC, but plans to begin marketing the app on social media for the rest of the year.

Ethereum Foundation Sounds Alarm Over AI Threats

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Ethereum Foundation has been working for years to secure the network against a future in which quantum computing breaks the cryptography underpinning Ethereum, but it is now facing a upcoming and more immediate concern around artificial intelligence.
  • AI is identifying bugs in live software more quickly than human reviewers can keep up with, and the Ethereum Foundation has now doubled the size of its protocol security team, according to a recent announcement.
  • As Kev Wedderburn wrote in a post from Devcon, AI models are now identifying thousands of bugs in the Linux kernel, one of the most scrutinized codebases in the world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Ethereum Foundation has been working for years to secure the network against a future in which quantum computing breaks the cryptography underpinning Ethereum, but it is now facing a upcoming and more immediate concern around artificial intelligence.

AI is identifying bugs in live software more quickly than human reviewers can keep up with, and the Ethereum Foundation has now doubled the size of its protocol security team, according to a recent announcement.

As Kev Wedderburn wrote in a post from Devcon, AI models are now identifying thousands of bugs in the Linux kernel, one of the most scrutinized codebases in the world.

For Ethereum developers, the immediate challenge is ensuring that bugs are not present in their software before an upgrade.

The longer-term challenge is mathematical. Ethereum uses digital signatures to identify who can spend funds and which validators have approved the state of the chain.

Wedderburn states that AI's advances in analyzing decades-old algorithms raise questions about the mathematical assumptions underlying those signatures that researchers should consider.

Sources indicate that it is not clear whether AI could break Ethereum's existing cryptography. However,  the Ethereum Foundation wants work on upcoming cryptography to be underway.

After more than a year of considering various signature schemes, the Ethereum Foundation has decided to replace elliptic-curve signatures with hash-based cryptography.

The argument is that Ethereum already relies on cryptographic hash security, and by using hashes for signatures too, it can remove an additional assumption about the difficulty of solving mathematical problems associated with elliptic curves.

The proposal affects three areas of Ethereum.

It would see validators use hash-based keys for their signatures, which in turn changes how block finality is determined on the network.

Wallet developers would need to provide owners with a way to transition their accounts to hash-based signatures.

And Ethereum's change to the cryptography used for commitments to data (blobs) that rollups publish to the network would require adjustments from rollups too.

According to recent reports, one challenge is the size of the signatures. Hash-based signatures are much larger, so developers need to consider how that affects the hardware needed to run a node at home.

Industry observers note that staking pools and multisig wallets would need adjustments too. So would smart contracts that rely on existing cryptography.

There will also be a need to adjust tools that rely on the signature scheme right now used by Ethereum validators (BLS).

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that base's Denim upgrade replaced Flashblocks with five canonical blocks per second.
  • In a recent development, for about sixteen months, Base's fastest blocks were only promises.
  • Denim went live on Base mainnet on November 5, after activating on Sepolia on October 21.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Industry observers note that base's Denim upgrade replaced Flashblocks with five canonical blocks per second. What that means for sequencers, RPC providers and smart contract developers is where the real story sits.

In a recent development, for about sixteen months, Base's fastest blocks were only promises. Since November 5, they are the ledger itself.

Denim went live on Base mainnet on November 5, after activating on Sepolia on October 21.

According to the upgrade page, the chain now produces five complete canonical blocks every second instead of one every two seconds. Flashblocks, the preconfirmation layer that ran alongside the two-second blocks since July 2025, is retired.

Most coverage stopped at the speed figure. The sharper question is what separates a canonical block from a preconfirmation, because that gap decides what breaks and what improves for anyone building on the chain.

It has been revealed that those updates were the sequencer's early word on what the next block would contain. They were previews of pending state, and nothing in them had its own hash, state root or receipts until the two-second block was sealed. Developers therefore had to keep an early execution result mentally separate from a settled transaction.

Denim turns the 200ms unit into the real thing. Under Base's 200ms Native Blocks specification, every block carries its own number, hash, state root, receipts and forkchoice updates, and moves through the unsafe, safe and finalized stages like any other block.

The sequencer's job gets heavier and stricter. Instead of streaming fragments of a larger block, it has to build and execute a full block for every 200ms slot. The header keeps its timestamp in whole seconds, so Denim adds a metadata transaction, the BaseTime deposit, placed second in every block. It supplies the sub-second portion: 0, 200, 400, 600 or 800 milliseconds.

Sources indicate that timing rules are tight. Slots can't be skipped, and each block's full timestamp must land exactly 200ms after its parent's. That timestamp comes from a schedule tied to the Denim activation and the block number, not from the sequencer's clock, so wall-clock time only determines when a build begins. Once execution finishes, the client rejects any block that breaks the 200ms progression.

In a recent development, this removes a layer of ambiguity. A preconfirmation was only as strong as the sequencer's word, while a canonical block can be validated, replayed and challenged by any node running the same derivation rules.

Industry observers note that app developers face the biggest practical shift. Flashblocks streams ended at activation, so anything built on newFlashblocks, pendingLogs or the pending block tag has to move to canonical subscriptions like newHeads and logs. The migration guide lists the API changes required.

Industry observers note that the seconds-based timestamp field stays as it was for compatibility. Block, header, transaction, log and receipt responses now include optional millisecond fields, timestampMs and blockTimestampMs, derived from authenticated BaseTime data. They are left out when that data has been pruned or is unavailable. One tooling detail deserves attention: the spec warns that the plain Alloy AnyRpcHeader type drops unknown fields, so anyone who needs millisecond timestamps must use a different type.

Industry observers note that node providers will see heavier traffic too. Dwellir's analysis notes that any service doing work on every block now does it ten times as often. Five fetches a second replace one every two seconds. Denim improves latency without adding capacity, so infrastructure bills are likely to climb.

Finality hasn't gone away either. Faster production doesn't erase the confirmation policy an application picks, and each 200ms block still passes through the same unsafe, safe and finalized stages. Bridges and exchanges that wait for a specific stage before crediting funds may need to rethink how many blocks they wait for, since a block count no longer equals the same stretch of time.

According to recent reports, this is the area that deserves the most urgent attention. Base's spec warns that block.number now advances ten times faster in real time, while block.timestamp still ticks in whole seconds. A contract that treats a block count as a duration will see that duration collapse to a tenth of what its authors intended.

According to recent reports, the affected patterns are common ones. Timelocks and cooldowns measured in blocks expire in a tenth of the time. Vesting and emission schedules run ten times faster. Per-block rate limits reset five times a second instead of once every two seconds, which lifts the effective per-second limit tenfold. Governance voting windows set in blocks shrink the same way. Uniswap V3-style TWAP oracles stay accurate, but a fixed observation cardinality now covers less wall-clock history, so long lookbacks can revert sooner.

In a recent development, contracts built on block.timestamp are unaffected. Where a block count can be adjusted through governance, teams plan to divide it by ten. Where it is hardcoded into an immutable contract, the spec says it can't be retuned after activation, which leaves migration as the only fix. Denim also tightens transfer rules for Base's B20 token standard, and transfers to a token's own address now revert.

Sources indicate that the coming weeks will show how much of this stays theoretical. Three things are worth tracking: whether any immutable contract with block-count logic misbehaves, how providers cope with the jump in per-block requests, and whether apps built around Flashblocks have fully moved over.

It has been revealed that denim looks like a cleaner design than the layer it replaced. A preview mechanism gives way to a block anyone can verify, and developers pay for it with a real migration. Speed grabbed the headlines, but the lasting change is that Base's sub-second confirmations now stand on the same footing as the chain's ordinary blocks.

Ethereum bulls face a frightening downside scenario after legendary trader and classical chart analyst Peter Brandt issued a fresh warning that the second-largest cryptocurrency could collapse below $500. His bearish outlook has raised fresh concerns about ETH’s ability to withstand mounting selling pressure, particularly as market uncertainty continues to weigh on investor sentiment.

In a November 24 post on X, Peter Brandt pointed to Ethereum’s deteriorating weekly chart structure, suggesting that ETH is approaching a critical point within a multi-year consolidation pattern.

The weekly chart above demonstrates a large symmetrical triangle that has formed over several market cycles. Its upper boundary is defined by a descending resistance line stretching from Ethereum’s November 2021 peak near $4,800, while the lower boundary consists of an ascending support line originating around the 2022 bear-market bottom.

Together, these converging trendlines have gradually narrowed Ethereum’s trading range, setting the stage for a potentially decisive breakout or breakdown.

Recent findings suggest that ETH briefly broke above the triangle’s upper resistance during its 2025 rally, eventually reaching a upcoming all-time high near $4,954 in August. However, the bullish breakout failed to produce a sustained upward move, with the cryptocurrency subsequently reversing direction.

The resulting decline has produced a series of lower highs and renewed selling pressure throughout 2026, bringing ETH increasingly close to the triangle’s lower boundary.

Brandt’s bearish outlook hinges on Ethereum losing its long-standing ascending support trendline, a development that could undermine a chart structure that has supported several significant recovery attempts since 2022.

Recent findings suggest that using $1,648 as the current reference price, ETH would need to shed approximately 16.1% to revisit the critical $1,383 support level. However, the classical chartist’s more alarming outlook points to a potential plunge below $500 if the cryptocurrency fails to defend this structural floor.

A drop from $1,648 to $500 would translate into a staggering 69.7% decline. Even if ETH first falls to $1,383, it would still face another 63.8% downside before reaching $500.

This distinction is vital because the sub-$500 projection represents a much deeper bearish scenario, not an automatic consequence of losing the immediate support level.

Such a collapse would also push Ethereum below its 2022 bear-market low, potentially marking a dramatic breakdown in its longer-term price structure.

According to recent reports, for Ethereum to begin reversing its bearish momentum, buyers must first push the altcoin king back above $1,715 and sustain a recovery beyond that threshold. Reclaiming this level would signal improving demand and offer an early sign that selling pressure is easing.

The next major hurdle sits around $1,840, which coincides with ETH’s November 23 rebound high. A decisive move above this resistance would help invalidate the recent pattern of lower highs and strengthen the case for a broader recovery.

Industry observers note that on the downside, a confirmed weekly close below $1,383—particularly if followed by an unsuccessful attempt to reclaim that level—would signal a potentially damaging breakdown of Ethereum’s multi-year ascending support structure. If that scenario unfolds, ETH could face renewed selling pressure toward the psychologically important $1,000 mark. A deeper deterioration in market conditions could then bring Brandt’s sub-$500 projection into sharper focus.

However, the bearish forecast remains conditional rather than inevitable. Ethereum has yet to lose the critical $1,383 support, leaving its ability to defend this level central to determining whether Brandt’s worst-case scenario becomes a reality.
